A bar has nodes \(0, 1, \dots, n\) in order along the axis \(x\) and elements \(1, \dots, n\), where element \(e\) has the nodes \(e - 1\) and \(e\), length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) and axial stiffness \(EA_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). Let \(\mat K\) be the structure matrix of theorem 7.13. Then

\[\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n} \frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(d_{\mathrm{e}} - d_{\mathrm{e}-1})^2 , \tag{7.14}\]

the matrix \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite, and \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\) if and only if \(\vek d = c\,(1, 1, \dots, 1)\) for some number \(c\).

Proof

We must show three things: the form of the energy, semidefiniteness and the kernel. We split the energy by elements, because the matrix is a sum of element contributions.

  1. By item 2 of theorem 7.13, \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = (d_{\mathrm{e}-1}, d_{\mathrm{e}})\).
  2. By lemma 7.5, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(d_{\mathrm{e}-1}^2 - 2 d_{\mathrm{e}-1} d_{\mathrm{e}} + d_{\mathrm{e}}^2) = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(d_{\mathrm{e}} - d_{\mathrm{e}-1})^2\). Summing over \(e\) gives equation (7.14).
  3. Every term of the sum is nonnegative, because \(EA_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) are positive, so \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d \ge 0\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric (corollary 7.14), hence positive semidefinite (definition 7.15).
  4. By lemma 7.16, \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\) if and only if \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\). A sum of nonnegative terms is zero if and only if every term is zero, so \(d_{\mathrm{e}} = d_{\mathrm{e}-1}\) for every \(e = 1, \dots, n\).
  5. From \(d_0 = d_1 = \dots = d_{\mathrm{n}}\) it follows that \(\vek d = c\,(1, \dots, 1)\) with \(c = d_0\). Conversely, for such \(\vek d\) every term of the sum is zero.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

For the example of equation (7.13), \(n = 2\), \(EA_{\mathrm{e}}/h_{\mathrm{e}} = 3{,}079 \cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 3{,}079 \cdot 10^6\,\big((d_1 - d_0)^2 + (d_2 - d_1)^2\big)\) N/m, as we expanded it before. The displacement of the bar as a whole is the only one that requires no force. For trusses in the plane and in space we will see that other displacements can also have zero energy. A displacement of the whole truss as a body and a rotation of the truss about a point stretch no bar (section 7.5), and this is exactly what the supports will have to prevent.

7.3.2 Supports and the reduced system (podpore in reducirani sistem)

The matrix \(\mat K\) of theorem 7.13 lacks a support. The weak form of chapter 6 says what to do with it. At a node where a support prescribes the displacement, the test functions are zero (definition 6.6), so we get no equation from there. Equations come only from test functions that are zero at all supported nodes, that is from the hat functions of the free nodes. We therefore divide the unknowns into two parts. A free unknown is the displacement of a node that no support prescribes, and a prescribed unknown is one whose value is given, for the hanging bar \(d_0 = 0\). We denote the free ones by the index \(\mathrm{f}\) and the prescribed ones by the index \(\mathrm{p}\). We renumber the unknowns so that the free ones come before the prescribed ones, and rearrange the rows and columns of the matrix in the same way. This is only a renaming of unknowns, which changes no equation and no value of \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d\), and the symmetry remains. The matrix, the columns of unknowns and the right-hand sides split into blocks:

\[\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{fp}} \\ \mat K_{\mathrm{pf}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{pp}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek d = \begin{pmatrix} \vek d_{\mathrm{f}} \\ \vek d_{\mathrm{p}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek f = \begin{pmatrix} \vek f_{\mathrm{f}} \\ \vek f_{\mathrm{p}} \end{pmatrix} . \tag{7.15}\]

The block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) has the rows and columns of the free unknowns, and the block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\) the rows of the free and the columns of the prescribed ones. For the hanging bar, \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is the matrix that remains when we strike out row and column \(0\) (figure 7.7).

When does the block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) have an inverse, that is, when are the supports sufficient? The answer is a theorem. It requires the supports to stop all displacements that the structure does not resist with any force.

Theorem 7.18 Reduced system (reducirani sistem)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\vek f\) be the matrix and the right-hand side of a structure of theorem 7.13 with element matrices that satisfy the hypothesis of corollary 7.14, let the unknowns be divided into free and prescribed as in equation (7.15), and let the values \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}}\) be given. Let the column \(\vek d\) with the given \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}}\) satisfy \((\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} = f_{\mathrm{i}}\) for every free unknown \(i\). Then \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\) is a solution of the system

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} . \tag{7.16}\]

For the bar of item 3 of theorem 7.13 the condition is satisfied by the displacements of the finite element solution, the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the given \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) for every free unknown \(i\). If there is no nonzero \(\vek d\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\), then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite, the system (7.16) has exactly one solution, and Gaussian elimination without row exchanges reaches it with all pivots positive.

Proof

We must show that the rows of the free unknowns give the system (7.16), that for the bar the finite element solution satisfies them, and that the hypothesis guarantees positive definiteness. The latter is then covered by theorem 6.29.

  1. The bar. The test function \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) of a free node is zero at all prescribed nodes, so by definition 6.6 it is a test function. The equation \(B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) is thus the equation that the weak form requires for every free unknown \(i\).
  2. We insert the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) into the first argument. The form \(B\) is linear in the first argument (definition 6.4), so \(B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}}\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) by theorem 7.13. The same theorem gives \(\ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = f_{\mathrm{i}}\). For the bar every row \(i\) of a free node is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}}\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = f_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is the hypothesis of the theorem.
  3. By hypothesis \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}}\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = f_{\mathrm{i}}\) for every free unknown \(i\). We split the sum over \(j\) into free and prescribed unknowns. By the rule for the product of matrices (definition 1.98, applied to blocks), the rows of the free unknowns are \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\). We move the term with the prescribed values to the right and obtain equation (7.16).
  4. The block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is symmetric because it is part of the symmetric matrix \(\mat K\) (corollary 7.14), \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = K_{\mathrm{ji}}\) also for free \(i, j\).
  5. Let \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\) be a column of free unknowns and \(\vek z = (\vek y, \vek 0)\) the column of all unknowns, which is nonzero and has \(\vek z_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\). By the rule for the product of matrices on blocks, \(\vek z^\T\mat K\,\vek z = \vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek y\), since the other three blocks multiply the zero column.
  6. By corollary 7.14, \(\vek z^\T\mat K\,\vek z \ge 0\), and by the hypothesis it is not zero, so \(\vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek y > 0\). The block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is therefore a positive definite matrix (definition 6.27), and the claim about the solution and the pivots is theorem 6.29.

Source: COOK (2.7-1) to (2.7-3), PDF p. 54, and (2.7-5) to (2.7-8), PDF pp. 55-56, FELIPPA (3.21) to (3.23), PDF p. 45 (»striking out« of rows and columns), ONATE1 (2.85), (2.86), PDF p. 98, EP (8.2.41), p. 542 (first row and first column omitted, a system with a known right-hand column remains). The proof in steps is not from the sources.

The proof showed that the reduced system is not a new procedure but the rows of the weak form that we had in chapter 6 for the free hat functions, and that the positive definiteness of the block follows from the condition on the supports. The condition in words: the supports must stop every displacement in which the energy would stay zero. For a bar this condition is simple.

Corollary 7.19 A supported bar (podprta palica)

Let the bar be as in lemma 7.17 and let at least one unknown be prescribed, \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\) for some \(k\). Then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite, the system (7.16) has exactly one solution, and elimination reaches it with positive pivots.

Proof

We must show that the hypothesis of theorem 7.18 holds.

  1. Let \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\). By lemma 7.16, \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\), so by lemma 7.17 \(\vek d = c\,(1, \dots, 1)\).
  2. The unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) is prescribed, so \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) in \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\). From \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = c\) it follows that \(c = 0\) and \(\vek d = \vek 0\), a contradiction.
  3. The hypothesis of theorem 7.18 therefore holds, and the claim is the theorem itself.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

For a bar the supports therefore cannot be chosen wrongly: any node with a given displacement suffices. For trusses the condition will be stricter and we will have to check it.

We test it on the hanging bar of two elements. The free unknowns are \(d_1\) and \(d_2\), the prescribed one is \(d_0 = 0\). The block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is the matrix that remains when we strike out row and column \(0\) of the matrix of equation (7.13), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\) is the column \(\frac{EA}{h}(-1, 0)\), and because of \(d_0 = 0\) we have \(\mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\). The system (7.16) is

\[\frac{EA}{h} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 30{,}05 \\ 15{,}02 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{N} . \tag{7.17}\]

Elimination starts with the pivot \(2EA/h = 6{,}158 \cdot 10^6\) N/m. We add half of the first row to the second and obtain \(\big(1 - \tfrac12\big)\frac{EA}{h}\,d_2 = 15{,}02 + \tfrac12\,30{,}05\) N. The second pivot is \(\frac{EA}{2h} = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, positive, as corollary 7.19 predicts, and the right-hand side is \(30{,}05\) N. From this \(d_2 = 30{,}05\ \text{N} / (1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m}) = 19{,}52\) µm. The first row gives \(d_1 = \big(30{,}05\ \text{N} + \frac{EA}{h}\,d_2\big) / (2EA/h) = 14{,}64\) µm. Both displacements are the same as in chapter 6 and are exact (theorem 6.38).

What happens if there is no support? Elimination of the whole matrix of equation (7.13) starts with the pivot \(\frac{EA}{h}\). After the first step \(\frac{EA}{h}\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) remains, the second pivot is again \(\frac{EA}{h}\), and after the second step the third entry is \(\frac{EA}{h}(1 - 1) = 0\). The third pivot is zero, we cannot divide, and elimination fails. The positive pivots of theorem 6.29 are lost exactly where the energy is zero.

7.3.3 A prescribed displacement that is not zero (predpisan pomik, ki ni nič)

A support often does not only hold a node but moves it. The foundation of a building can settle, or a structure can be deliberately clamped into a displaced support. Does theorem 7.18 cover this? It does, because it does not require \(\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\). Take the bar of chapter 6 fixed at both ends (subsection 6.4.2), where the lower support has settled by \(\bar u = 0{,}1\) mm downward. The bar has the same data as before and two elements, nodes \(0\), \(1\), \(2\). The prescribed ones are \(d_0 = 0\) and \(d_2 = \bar u\), only \(d_1\) is free. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is a single entry, \(K_{11} = 2EA/h = 6{,}158 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, and the row \(\mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\) is \(\big(K_{10}, K_{12}\big) = \frac{EA}{h}(-1, -1)\). The term with the prescribed values is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} = -\frac{EA}{h}\,\bar u\), and equation (7.16) is

\[\frac{2EA}{h}\,d_1 = f_1 + \frac{EA}{h}\,\bar u = 30{,}05\ \text{N} + 307{,}88\ \text{N} = 337{,}93\ \text{N} , \tag{7.18}\]

where \(EA\,\bar u/h = 3{,}079 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 307{,}88\) N. From this \(d_1 = 54{,}88\) µm.

We check against the known solution. The true field of this problem is \(a\,x\,(L - x) + \bar u\,x/L\) (subsection 6.4.2), at the middle \(x = 5\) m it is \(a \cdot 25\ \text{m}^2 + \bar u/2 = 4{,}88\ \text{µm} + 50{,}00\ \text{µm} = 54{,}88\) µm, the same number. Equation (7.18) gives it in two parts: \(30{,}05\ \text{N}/(6{,}158 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m}) = 4{,}88\) µm from the weight and \(307{,}88\ \text{N}/(6{,}158 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m}) = 50{,}00\) µm from the settlement, that is half of the settlement, because node \(1\) is in the middle between the supports.

Why did \(307{,}88\) N appear on the right-hand side? Imagine that we clamp the second element at its lower end into the displaced support and hold node \(1\) at \(d_1 = 0\). The element stretches by \(\bar u\) and pulls node \(1\) downward with the force \(EA\,\bar u/h\). When solving for the free node we must subtract this force, so on the right-hand side we add it as a load (figure 7.8). The prescribed displacement acts on the free node as a load equal to the force that would be needed to stretch the element by this displacement while the free node is held.

In a computer program, splitting the matrix into blocks is laborious, because the rows and columns would have to be rearranged. A procedure that keeps the size of the system is therefore often used (COOK, PDF pp. 54-55, »without ... changing its size, or rearranging its terms«). For every prescribed unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\) we do three things: from the right-hand side of every other row \(i\) we subtract \(K_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\), we replace the row and column \(k\) of the matrix by zeros and put \(1\) on the diagonal, and on the right-hand side of row \(k\) we put \(\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let us prove that the solution is the same.

Row \(k\) of the new matrix is \((0, \dots, 1, \dots, 0)\) and the right-hand side is \(\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\), so the equation says \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is exactly the prescribed value. Row \(i\) of a free node has a zero in column \(k\), so it no longer contains the unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\), and on the right-hand side it has \(f_{\mathrm{i}} - K_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\). This is row \(i\) of the system (7.16), in which the term \(K_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\) has been moved to the right. Only the rows \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\), which do not mix unknowns, have been added to the free rows, so the solution for the free unknowns is the same as for equation (7.16). For the settled bar of equation (7.18) the nodes \(0\) and \(2\) are prescribed. The new matrix is diagonal,

\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2EA/h & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} d_0 \\ d_1 \\ d_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 337{,}93\ \text{N} \\ \bar u \end{pmatrix} , \tag{7.19}\]

and from it we read \(d_0 = 0\), \(d_1 = 337{,}93\ \text{N}/(2EA/h) = 54{,}88\) µm, \(d_2 = \bar u\). The matrix is still symmetric, which preserves the advantage of symmetric storage. The ones on the diagonal have a different unit than \(2EA/h\) in N/m, which is unpleasant for large structures. COOK mentions as an alternative that the original \(K_{\mathrm{kk}}\) stays on the diagonal and \(K_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\) goes to the right-hand side of row \(k\) (COOK, PDF p. 55). The solution is again the same, because row \(k\) again says \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d_{\mathrm{k}}\), only with both sides multiplied by \(K_{\mathrm{kk}}\).

Prescribed values can also be imposed in two other ways, with a penalty (penalty method) and with Lagrange multipliers. COOK only mentions them: »Boundary conditions can also be treated by Lagrange multipliers and by the penalty method« (COOK, PDF p. 56). We will meet the penalty in frames in chapter 12, and the multipliers in chapter 8, where they appear as constraint forces. In this chapter we stay with the division into blocks and with the procedure that keeps the size.

7.3.4 Reactions (reakcije)

The reduced system does not use the rows of the prescribed unknowns. We must not throw these rows away, because they hold the forces with which the supports hold the structure. A reaction is the force that a support exerts on the structure at the node of a prescribed unknown, in the direction of that unknown. How do we obtain it?

Row \(i\) of the product \(\mat K\,\vek d\) is the force that we must give to node \(i\) from outside to maintain the displacements \(\vek d\). Column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is namely the force at the nodes that is needed for a unit displacement of unknown \(j\) with the other unknowns zero (definition 7.4), and row \(i\) of the product is the sum of these contributions at the given \(d_{\mathrm{j}}\). At a free node this force is provided by the load, and \((\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} = f_{\mathrm{i}}\) is exactly an equation of the system. At a prescribed node the load \(f_{\mathrm{i}}\) carries a part, and the remainder must be provided by the support. The reaction is therefore the difference

\[r_{\mathrm{i}} = (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} - f_{\mathrm{i}} , \qquad i \text{ prescribed} ,\]

which for the blocks of equation (7.15) means

\[\vek r_{\mathrm{p}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{pf}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{pp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{p}} . \tag{7.20}\]

At free unknowns there is no support, \(r_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), and all the conditions together are written as \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\) with a column \(\vek r\) that is nonzero only at the prescribed unknowns. The reactions are computed afterwards and do not influence the solution for the displacements, since the free system of equation (7.16) does not contain the prescribed rows. ONATE1 says in words that the reactions are computed »a posteriori« from the already known displacements (ONATE1 (2.26), PDF p. 74, and (2.85), PDF p. 98), EP with the row that remains unused when the first row and column are omitted and from which we get the unknown reaction (EP (8.2.41) and (8.2.45), pp. 542-543), FELIPPA multiplies the whole solution by the matrix and obtains the reactions besides the known loads (FELIPPA (3.26), PDF p. 46), COOK obtains them by multiplying the solution by the rows of the matrix that were discarded when the supports were entered (COOK, PDF p. 56).

The hanging bar of two elements. Only \(d_0 = 0\) is prescribed, row \(0\) of the matrix of equation (7.13) is \(\frac{EA}{h}(1, -1, 0)\), and \((\mat K\,\vek d)_0 = \frac{EA}{h}\,(d_0 - d_1) = -3{,}079 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot 14{,}64\ \text{µm} = -45{,}07\) N. The load of the node is \(f_0 = 15{,}02\) N, so

\[r_0 = -45{,}073\ \text{N} - 15{,}024\ \text{N} = -60{,}097\ \text{N} .\]

The support pulls the bar upward (the axis points down) with the force \(60{,}097\) N, which is the weight of the whole bar \(qL = 6{,}0097 \cdot 10 = 60{,}097\) N. The settled bar has two reactions. Rows \(0\) and \(2\) of the matrix are \(\frac{EA}{h}(1, -1, 0)\) and \(\frac{EA}{h}(0, -1, 1)\), and with \(d = (0,\ 54{,}88\ \text{µm},\ 100{,}00\ \text{µm})\) we get \((\mat K\,\vek d)_0 = -3{,}0788 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 54{,}88 \cdot 10^{-6} = -168{,}96\) N and \((\mat K\,\vek d)_2 = 3{,}0788 \cdot 10^6 \cdot (100{,}00 - 54{,}88) \cdot 10^{-6} = 138{,}92\) N. After subtracting the loads \(f_0 = f_2 = 15{,}02\) N, computed with unrounded values,

\[r_0 = -183{,}99\ \text{N} , \qquad r_2 = 123{,}89\ \text{N} .\]

The upper support pulls upward with \(183{,}99\) N, and the lower one pulls downward with \(123{,}89\) N, because the settlement stretches the bar at its lower end. The sum of the reactions is \(-60{,}10\) N, again the weight of the bar. Is this a coincidence?

Lemma 7.20 Balance of reactions and loads (ravnovesje reakcij in bremen)

Let \(\vek d\) be a solution of the reduced system of a bar from theorem 7.18 and \(\vek r = \mat K\,\vek d - \vek f\) the column of reactions, which is zero at free unknowns. Then

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} r_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \tag{7.21}\]

the sum over all nodes: the reactions are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the sum of all nodal loads.

Proof

We must show that the column of ones \(\vek 1 = (1, \dots, 1)\) is multiplied by \(\mat K\) into zero, and that this gives the claim when the equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\) is multiplied from the left.

  1. By lemma 7.6, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(1, 1) = \vek 0\) for every element. The selection matrix picks from \(\vek 1\) the two components that belong to element \(e\), these are ones, \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek 1 = (1, 1)\), so by theorem 7.13 \(\mat K\,\vek 1 = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(1, 1) = \vek 0\).
  2. For free unknowns the row is an equation of (7.16), and for prescribed ones it is the definition of the column \(\vek r\). Together \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\) holds.
  3. We multiply the equation from the left by the row \(\vek 1^\T\): \(\vek 1^\T\mat K\,\vek d = \vek 1^\T\vek f + \vek 1^\T\vek r\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric (corollary 7.14), so by lemma 1.101 \(\vek 1^\T\mat K = (\mat K^\T\vek 1)^\T = (\mat K\,\vek 1)^\T = \vek 0^\T\) by step 1. The left-hand side is zero, and the right-hand side is \(\vek 1^\T\vek f + \vek 1^\T\vek r = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} r_{\mathrm{i}}\), which is equation (7.21).

Source: The proof is not from a source in this form. FELIPPA, PDF p. 46: »It is easy to check that the complete force system is in equilibrium«.

The proof showed that the reactions and the loads are in balance because a rigid displacement of the bar needs no force, that is because of the same zero energy that cost the matrix \(\mat K\) its inverse. We check on the examples: hanging bar \(15{,}024 + 30{,}049 + 15{,}024 - 60{,}097 = 0\), settled bar \(15{,}024 + 30{,}049 + 15{,}024 - 183{,}989 + 123{,}892 = 0\) (node \(1\) is not supported and has \(r_1 = 0\)). So checking the reactions is the first thing we do after a computation: the sum of the reactions must be opposite to the sum of the loads. The check is necessary but not sufficient. The reactions would satisfy equation (7.21) even with a wrongly computed stiffness, as we will see for the bridge in section 7.7.

For the hanging bar the lemma itself says that the only reaction is \(r_0 = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}} = -qL\), because this is the only supported unknown. The sum of the nodal loads is the whole load, because on every element the two shape functions add up to \(1\) (lemma 7.3), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}} = \ell\big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\big) = \int_0^L q\,\mathrm{d}x = qL\). Therefore the reaction is exact for every number of elements. The computation for \(n = 1\), \(2\), \(4\) elements (SymPy and NumPy) always gives \(-60{,}097\) N. For the settled bar two unknowns are supported, the lemma gives only the sum, and each reaction separately should be exact too. Why?

Let us also look at the force in an element. By section 7.1.4, \(N_{\mathrm{e}} = EA\,(d_{\mathrm{e}} - d_{\mathrm{e}-1})/h\) is constant on the element. For the bar of two elements \(N_1 = 3{,}079 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 14{,}64 \cdot 10^{-6} = 45{,}07\) N and \(N_2 = 3{,}079 \cdot 10^6 \cdot (19{,}52 - 14{,}64) \cdot 10^{-6} = 15{,}02\) N. The true axial force is \(N(x) = q\,(L - x)\), at the support \(N(0) = qL = 60{,}10\) N. The force in the first element is \(45{,}07\) N, so \(qh/2 = 15{,}02\) N too little, exactly as much as \(f_0\). For four elements the forces are \(52{,}585\), \(37{,}561\), \(22{,}536\) and \(7{,}512\) N, each is the average of the true force \(q\,(L - x)\) on its element. The first average is \(q\,(L - h/2)\), so \(N_1 = N(0) - qh/2\). Therefore from the equation \(r_0 = (\mat K\,\vek d)_0 - f_0 = -N_1 - f_0\) it follows that

\[r_0 = -\big(N_1 + f_0\big) = -\big(N(0) - qh/2 + qh/2\big) = -N(0) . \tag{7.22}\]

The support carries the force of the first element and that part of the weight that hangs on node \(0\). The force in the element at the support is inexact by \(qh/2\), and the reaction is exact, because the missing part is added to it by the load of the node. This holds more generally.

The reaction is exact if the displacements of both nodes of the first element are exact. For the hanging bar this is guaranteed by theorem 6.38. For a bar fixed at both ends that theorem says nothing, because it is written for a single support at \(x = 0\), so we prove the exactness of the nodes separately. The proof follows the same idea: the error is orthogonal to the hat functions of the free nodes, and from this it follows that the error at all nodes is zero.

Lemma 7.21 Exact nodal displacements of a bar fixed at both ends (točni pomiki vozlišč palice, pritrjene na obeh koncih)

A bar has nodes \(0, 1, \dots, n\) at \(0 = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{n}} = L\) and elements \([x_{\mathrm{e}-1}, x_{\mathrm{e}}]\) with length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = x_{\mathrm{e}} - x_{\mathrm{e}-1}\) and axial stiffness \(EA_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\), which is constant on each element (so there is a node wherever \(EA\) changes). The load \(q\) is continuous on each element. The displacements \(d_0\) and \(d_{\mathrm{n}}\) are prescribed. Let \(u\) be a piecewise continuously differentiable solution of the weak form with \(u(0) = d_0\) and \(u(L) = d_{\mathrm{n}}\), and \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{j}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) the finite element solution of theorem 7.18, where the free unknowns are \(d_1, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}-1}\). Then \(d_{\mathrm{j}} = u(x_{\mathrm{j}})\) for every \(j = 0, 1, \dots, n\).

Proof

We must show that the error \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is zero at all nodes. The hat function of every free node is orthogonal to the error, which gives equal forces in neighbouring elements, and the two ends close them.

  1. The function \(e\) is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable on the same partition as \(u\) and \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). Since \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = 1\) for \(j = i\) and \(0\) for \(j \ne i\) (definition 6.25), \(u_{\mathrm{h}}(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = d_{\mathrm{i}}\), so \(e(x_0) = d_0 - u(0) = 0\) and \(e(x_{\mathrm{n}}) = d_{\mathrm{n}} - u(L) = 0\). We write \(e_{\mathrm{j}} = e(x_{\mathrm{j}})\).
  2. For \(k = 1, \dots, n - 1\) the function \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero at \(x_0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\), so it is a test function (definition 6.6), hence \(B(u, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\). The unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) is free, so by theorem 7.18 \(B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\). By linearity of \(B\) in the first argument, \(B(e, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\).
  3. On element \(k\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}' = 1/h_{\mathrm{k}}\), on element \(k + 1\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}' = -1/h_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), and elsewhere zero (definition 6.25). Since \(EA\) is constant on each element, by lemma 6.12
    \[\begin{aligned} B(e, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) &= \frac{EA_{\mathrm{k}}}{h_{\mathrm{k}}}\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} e'\,\mathrm{d}x - \frac{EA_{\mathrm{k}+1}}{h_{\mathrm{k}+1}}\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{k}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}+1}} e'\,\mathrm{d}x = s_{\mathrm{k}} - s_{\mathrm{k}+1} , \\ s_{\mathrm{j}} = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{j}}}{h_{\mathrm{j}}}\,(e_{\mathrm{j}} - e_{\mathrm{j}-1}) . \end{aligned}\]
  4. From steps 2 and 3, \(s_1 = s_2 = \dots = s_{\mathrm{n}}\). We denote this number by \(s\).
  5. From the definition of \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(e_{\mathrm{j}} - e_{\mathrm{j}-1} = s\,h_{\mathrm{j}}/EA_{\mathrm{j}}\). The sum over \(j = 1, \dots, n\) gives \(e_{\mathrm{n}} - e_0 = s \sum_{\mathrm{j}} h_{\mathrm{j}}/EA_{\mathrm{j}}\). The left-hand side is zero by step 1, the sum on the right is positive, so \(s = 0\).
  6. From \(s = 0\) it follows that \(e_{\mathrm{j}} = e_{\mathrm{j}-1}\) for every \(j\), so \(e_{\mathrm{j}} = e_0 = 0\) and \(d_{\mathrm{j}} = u_{\mathrm{h}}(x_{\mathrm{j}}) = u(x_{\mathrm{j}})\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The same reason as in theorem 6.38, which is written for one support.

For \(n = 1\) there are no free unknowns, step 4 says nothing and step 5 gives \(s = 0\) directly. For the settled bar of two elements \(n = 2\) and the lemma says that \(d_1 = 54{,}88\) µm is the exact value, which we checked earlier against the known solution.

Lemma 7.22 Exactness of the reaction of a bar (točnost reakcije palice)

Let the bar have the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\), loaded only by a piecewise continuous distributed load \(q\), with piecewise continuous axial stiffness \(EA > 0\) that is constant on the first element \([x_0, x_1]\), \(x_0 = 0\), and let it be supported at \(x = 0\) (prescribed displacement). Let \(u\) be the solution of the weak form whose axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable with \(N' = -q\) (equilibrium of a bar element, chapter 6), \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) the finite element solution with the same value \(u(0)\), and let \(u_{\mathrm{h}}(x_0) = u(x_0)\) and \(u_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1) = u(x_1)\). Then the reaction at node \(0\) equals the exact reaction,

\[r_0 = -N(0) . \tag{7.23}\]
Proof

We must show that the error \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\) contributes nothing to the reaction. We write the reaction with the weak form tested with the hat function of the supported node, which is not a test function.

  1. Let \(\varphi = \psi_0\) be the hat function of node \(0\) (definition 6.25). We have \(\varphi(0) = 1\), \(\varphi = 0\) from \(x_1\) onward and \(\varphi' = -1/h_1\) on the first element of length \(h_1 = x_1 - x_0\).
  2. In the finite element method \(r_0 = (\mat K\,\vek d)_0 - f_0\), and row \(0\) is by theorem 7.13 \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_0)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} - \ell(\psi_0)\). By linearity of \(B\) in the first argument, \(r_0 = B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \varphi) - \ell(\varphi)\).
  3. For the exact solution \(B(u, \varphi) = \int_0^L N\,\varphi'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By lemma 6.13 with \(N' = -q\) and \(\varphi(L) = 0\) this is \(-N(0)\,\varphi(0) + \int_0^L q\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}x = -N(0) + \ell(\varphi)\). So \(-N(0) = B(u, \varphi) - \ell(\varphi)\).
  4. We subtract: \(r_0 - (-N(0)) = B(u_{\mathrm{h}}, \varphi) - B(u, \varphi) = -B(e, \varphi)\) by linearity of \(B\) in the first argument.
  5. Since \(\varphi' = 0\) outside the first element and \(EA\) is constant there, \(B(e, \varphi) = \int_0^{x_1} EA\,e'\,\varphi'\,\mathrm{d}x = -\frac{EA}{h_1}\,\big(e(x_1) - e(x_0)\big) = 0\), because \(e(x_0) = 0\) and \(e(x_1) = 0\) by assumption (lemma 6.12). Hence \(r_0 = -N(0)\).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The proof showed that the reaction stays exact whenever the displacements of both nodes of the first element are exact, no matter how the function differs between them. This is so for the hanging bar (the exactness of the displacements is guaranteed by theorem 6.38) and also for the settled bar (lemma 7.21). There the support is also at \(x = L\) and the same computation with the hat function \(\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) on the last element, where \(\psi_{\mathrm{n}}' = 1/h_{\mathrm{n}}\), gives in step 3 \(B(u, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}) = N(L) + \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{n}})\) and therefore \(r_2 = N(L)\). The exact force in the bar with the settlement is \(N = EA\,\big(a\,(L - 2x) + \bar u/L\big)\) (subsection 6.4.2), so \(N(0) = 183{,}99\) N and \(N(L) = 123{,}89\) N, and both agree with the reactions \(-183{,}99\) N and \(123{,}89\) N from the computation above. At node \(0\) the reaction thus receives all the accuracy of the displacements, while the force in the element at the support receives only the average.

We now have everything for the computation of a bar with linear elements. We eliminate the supported node (theorem 7.18), move a displacement that is not zero to the right-hand side, solve the system with positive pivots (theorem 6.29), then obtain the reactions from the rows of the supported nodes and check their sum (lemma 7.20). What remains open is what to do when the load varies along the element and straight lines on the element are too coarse. The answer is an element with more nodes, section 7.4.

7.4 The quadratic element and Gauss integration (kvadratni element in Gaussovo integriranje)

The linear element gives a constant axial force on each element. When the load along the bar varies, the true axial force varies too, and a stepped approximation follows it only as the number of elements grows. What do we gain if on each element we take a parabola instead of a line, and how do we compute the integrals that the parabola brings when they are no longer simple? First we write the element with three nodes, its matrix and its forces. Then we look for a way in which a computer evaluates integrals that we cannot write in closed form, and we show what happens if this way is chosen too sparingly. At the end we measure how fast the approximation improves as the elements are made smaller. We stay with the bar of chapter 6, with one displacement per node.

7.4.1 The element with three nodes (element s tremi vozlišči)

The quadratic element (kvadratni element) is a finite element (definition 7.1) with nodes at both ends and in the middle, at \(x = 0\), \(h/2\) and \(h\), where \(h\) is the length of the element. The column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (d_1, d_2, d_3)\) holds the displacements of these three nodes. The field on the element is a quadratic polynomial that takes these values at the nodes. We write it with the shape functions (definition 7.2), which are now quadratic polynomials, equal to \(1\) at their own node and to zero at the other two. The function \(\psi_2\) must have zeros at \(x = 0\) and \(x = h\), so \(\psi_2 = c\,x\,(x - h)\), and the condition \(\psi_2(h/2) = 1\) gives \(c\,(h/2)(-h/2) = 1\), so \(c = -4/h^2\). In the same way \(\psi_1\) has zeros at \(h/2\) and \(h\), so \(\psi_1 = c\,(x - h/2)(x - h)\) with \(c\,(-h/2)(-h) = 1\), so \(c = 2/h^2\), and \(\psi_3\) has zeros at \(0\) and \(h/2\), so \(\psi_3 = c\,x\,(x - h/2)\) with \(c\,h\,(h/2) = 1\), so again \(c = 2/h^2\). The results are

\[\begin{aligned} \psi_1 &= \frac{2\,(x - h/2)(x - h)}{h^2} , \qquad \psi_2 = -\frac{4\,x\,(x - h)}{h^2} , \\ \psi_3 &= \frac{2\,x\,(x - h/2)}{h^2} , \end{aligned} \tag{7.24}\]

drawn in figure 7.10. The field on the element is \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \psi_1 d_1 + \psi_2 d_2 + \psi_3 d_3\), and at a node it equals the displacement of that node. The same polynomials are written in ONATE1 (3.11), PDF p. 103, with the coordinate \(\xi = 2x/h - 1\), and in EP (8.2.18), p. 535, with the nodes \(x_1, x_2, x_3\).

The sum of the shape functions is \(1\) here too. In the computation, \(2x^2 - 3hx + h^2\) remains for \(\psi_1 h^2\), \(-4x^2 + 4hx\) for \(\psi_2 h^2\) and \(2x^2 - hx\) for \(\psi_3 h^2\), and their sum is \(h^2\). If all three nodes have the same displacement \(c\), then \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = c\) on the whole element: a rigid shift of the element gives no deformation, as for the linear element (lemma 7.3).

What changes? The derivatives \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\) are no longer constant but linear, so the strain \(u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) and the axial force \(N_{\mathrm{h}} = EA\,u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) are linear functions on the element. How this affects the computation is shown by the hanging bar (section 7.2.3). Before we try it, we compute the matrix and the forces of the element.

Lemma 7.23 Stiffness matrix and forces of the quadratic element (togostna matrika in sile kvadratnega elementa)

Let a quadratic element of length \(h\) have axial stiffness \(EA\), constant on the element, and let the load \(q\) along the axis be constant. Then its stiffness matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.4) and the vector of consistent nodal forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.7) are

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA}{3h} \begin{pmatrix} 7 & -8 & 1 \\ -8 & 16 & -8 \\ 1 & -8 & 7 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{q\,h}{6} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{7.25}\]

For a column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathsf T}\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) exactly when \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = c\,(1, 1, 1)\), and then \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} \vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\).

Proof

We must show four things: the values of the entries of \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), the values of the entries of \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\), the zero column, and that there is no other zero column.

  1. Differentiating equation (7.24) gives \(\psi_1' = (4x - 3h)/h^2\), \(\psi_2' = (4h - 8x)/h^2\), \(\psi_3' = (4x - h)/h^2\). The sum is \(0\), because the sum of the shape functions is constant.
  2. The entry \(k_{\mathrm{ij}} = \int_0^h EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\) is an integral of a polynomial of degree 2 (lemma 7.5, which writes the same matrix for the linear element). By lemma 3.39 and the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40), \(k_{11} = \frac{EA}{h^4}\int_0^h (16x^2 - 24hx + 9h^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{EA}{h}\,(\tfrac{16}{3} - 12 + 9) = \frac{7\,EA}{3h}\).
  3. In the same way \(k_{12} = \frac{EA}{h^4}\int_0^h (-32x^2 + 40hx - 12h^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{EA}{h}\,(-\tfrac{32}{3} + 20 - 12) = -\frac{8\,EA}{3h}\), \(k_{13} = \frac{EA}{h^4}\int_0^h (16x^2 - 16hx + 3h^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{EA}{h}\,(\tfrac{16}{3} - 8 + 3) = \frac{EA}{3h}\) and \(k_{22} = \frac{EA}{h^4}\int_0^h (64x^2 - 64hx + 16h^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{EA}{h}\,(\tfrac{64}{3} - 32 + 16) = \frac{16\,EA}{3h}\).
  4. The sum of row \(i\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} k_{\mathrm{ij}} = \int_0^h EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}' \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) by step 1. Therefore \(k_{23} = -k_{21} - k_{22} = -8EA/(3h)\) and \(k_{33} = -k_{31} - k_{32} = 7EA/(3h)\), where \(k_{31} = k_{13}\) and \(k_{32} = k_{23}\) because \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric. This gives all entries of the matrix, and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} (1, 1, 1)^{\mathsf T} = \vek 0\).
  5. The force is \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = \int_0^h q\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). For \(\psi_2\) we have \(\int_0^h \psi_2\,\mathrm{d}x = -\frac{4}{h^2}\,(\tfrac{h^3}{3} - \tfrac{h^3}{2}) = \tfrac{2h}{3}\). Since \(\psi_3(x) = \psi_1(h - x)\), \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_3\) have the same integral, and since the sum of the integrals of all three is \(\int_0^h 1\,\mathrm{d}x = h\), each of them is \(h/6\). So \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = q\,(h/6, 2h/3, h/6)\).
  6. Let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathsf T}\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = EA \int_0^h (u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). The derivative \(u_{\mathrm{h}}' = a + b\,x\) is linear, and the integral of its square is \(\int_0^h (a + bx)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = h\,\big((a + bh/2)^2 + b^2h^2/12\big)\). This sum of two squares is zero only for \(b = 0\) and \(a = 0\), so \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is constant on the element and all three nodal displacements are equal. Conversely, by step 4, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,c\,(1, 1, 1)^{\mathsf T} = \vek 0\).

Source: ONATE1 (3.36) and (3.37), PDF p. 111, which writes the matrix as \(\frac{EA}{6l}\) times the matrix with entries \(14, -16, 2, 32\), so the same matrix, and EP (8.2.32), p. 539, in the form \(\frac{EA}{3h}\) times the matrix with entries \(7, -8, 1, 16\) and \(\frac{qh}{6}\,(1, 4, 1)\). The proof in steps is ours.

The eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA/h)\) are \(0\), \(2\) and \(8\) (SymPy). The zero belongs to the rigid shift, and the lemma says that this is the only direction without energy. We test it on the hanging bar of section 7.2.3. Its length is \(L = 10\) m, its axial stiffness \(EA = 1{,}5394 \cdot 10^7\) N, its self weight \(q = 6{,}0097\) N/m, the upper end is fixed and the lower end is free. Take a single quadratic element, \(h = L\). By equation (7.25) the forces of the element are \((10{,}016, 40{,}065, 10{,}016)\) N, and their sum is \(q L = 60{,}097\) N. The upper node is fixed, so we strike out the first row and column. The system that remains is

\[\frac{EA}{3h} \begin{pmatrix} 16 & -8 \\ -8 & 7 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 40{,}065 \\ 10{,}016 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{N} , \tag{7.26}\]

with \(EA/(3h) = 5{,}1313 \cdot 10^5\) N/m. The solution is \(d_2 = 14{,}640\) µm and \(d_3 = 19{,}520\) µm, and these are the exact displacements of the middle and the end of the hanging bar (section 6.4.2). For this load the true displacement is the quadratic polynomial \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), which lies in the field of the quadratic element, so the element gives the true field everywhere, not only at the nodes (the same is shown by ONATE1, example 3.4, PDF p. 123). The axial force \(N_{\mathrm{h}} = EA\,u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) is linear and equal to the true one, \(N = q\,(L - x)\): \(60{,}10\) N at \(x = 0\), \(45{,}07\) N at \(2{,}5\) m, \(30{,}05\) N at \(5\) m, \(15{,}02\) N at \(7{,}5\) m and zero at \(x = L\) (SymPy). The linear element with two elements gave \(45{,}07\) N and \(15{,}02\) N, with four elements \(52{,}59\) N at the support. The reaction from the first row, \(r = (EA/3h)(-8 d_2 + d_3) - q h/6\), is \(-60{,}097\) N, equal to the weight of the bar.

Why is the middle force \(4qh/6\), but \(q h/6\) at the ends? A naive division would assign to each node the load of the part of the element nearest to it, so \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac12\), \(\tfrac14\) of the weight \(q h\). The consistent forces are the work of the load on the field of the element, \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = \int q\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), so the areas under the shape functions multiplied by \(q\). The area under \(\psi_2\) is \(2h/3\), under \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_3\) only \(h/6\) each, because \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_3\) have negative parts that reduce the area (figure 7.11). The middle node therefore carries four times as much load as an end node (ONATE1, PDF p. 111, which calls this a result that is not the obvious one and a consequence of the principle of virtual work and the quadratic approximation). Together the areas give \(h\), so the sum of the forces is equal to the weight \(q h\).

What if we do not load the middle node? Then the second equation of the element is \(\tfrac{EA}{3h}\,(-8d_1 + 16d_2 - 8d_3) = 0\), so \(d_2 = (d_1 + d_3)/2\). If we eliminate the middle displacement (the same elimination step as in section 6.3.4, except that the pivot is the middle entry \(16\) instead of the first), what remains is

\[\begin{aligned} &\frac{EA}{3h}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 1 \\ 1 & 7 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{16} \begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -8 & -8 \end{pmatrix} \right) \\ &\quad = \frac{EA}{3h} \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{EA}{h} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \end{aligned} \tag{7.27}\]

the matrix of the linear element. Without a load along the element the third node therefore adds nothing, because the true solution is then linear (\(EA\,u'' = 0\)) and the middle displacement is the mean of the two end ones, which a line already has. The third node pays off only under a load along the element.

7.4.2 Mathematics: Gauss integration (Gaussovo integriranje)

For a quadratic element with constant stiffness the integrals are polynomials of degree two, which we know how to compute. When the stiffness or the load varies along the element by a complicated law, or when the middle node is not in the middle of the element, the integrands contain rational functions and the integral is no longer simple (ONATE1, PDF p. 111). A computer program does not compute a primitive function but replaces each element integral by a sum of values of the integrand at a few points. How do we choose the points and the weights so that the sum equals the integral for as many integrands as possible?

First the unit interval. The element \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) with midpoint \(x_{\mathrm{m}} = (x_{\mathrm{a}} + x_{\mathrm{b}})/2\) and length \(h\) is mapped to \([-1, 1]\) by \(x = x_{\mathrm{m}} + \xi\,h/2\). Let \(g\) be a continuous function on the element, extended to the left of \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) by the constant value \(g(x_{\mathrm{a}})\) and to the right of \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\) by the constant value \(g(x_{\mathrm{b}})\), so that it is continuous on an open interval containing the element, and \(G\) its primitive function, which exists by theorem 3.40, item 2. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43, the special case of a function \(G\) that does not depend on the other coordinates, along a curve on the \(x\) axis, with \(G\) continuously differentiable because \(G' = g\) is continuous), \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\xi}\,G(x_{\mathrm{m}} + \xi h/2) = g(x_{\mathrm{m}} + \xi h/2)\,\tfrac h2\), so by item 1 of the same theorem

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} g\,\mathrm{d}x = G(x_{\mathrm{b}}) - G(x_{\mathrm{a}}) = \frac h2 \int_{-1}^{1} g\big(x_{\mathrm{m}} + \xi\,\tfrac h2\big)\,\mathrm{d}\xi . \tag{7.28}\]

The factor \(h/2\) is the ratio of lengths \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}\xi\). For the quadratic element \(x_{\mathrm{m}} = h/2\), and the shape functions in \(\xi\) are \(N_1 = \xi(\xi - 1)/2\), \(N_2 = 1 - \xi^2\), \(N_3 = \xi(\xi + 1)/2\) (ONATE1 (3.11), PDF p. 103), which on substituting \(x = h(1 + \xi)/2\) into equation (7.24) gives exactly the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\). The derivative with respect to \(x\) is \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}' = \tfrac2h\,N_{\mathrm{i}}'\), where the prime denotes the derivative with respect to \(\xi\), so by equation (7.28)

\[\begin{aligned} k_{\mathrm{ij}} &= \int_0^h EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{2\,EA}{h} \int_{-1}^{1} N_{\mathrm{i}}'\,N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}\xi , \\ N_1' &= \xi - \tfrac12 , \quad N_2' = -2\xi , \quad N_3' = \xi + \tfrac12 . \end{aligned} \tag{7.29}\]

The integrands are polynomials of degree two in \(\xi\).

Now the sum. Take a function \(g\) on \([-1, 1]\) and points \(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_{\mathrm{q}}\) with weights \(w_1, \dots, w_{\mathrm{q}}\). The simplest demand is that the sum \(\sum w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\) gives the true integral for as many powers \(1, \xi, \xi^2, \dots\) as possible. Since we can choose \(q\) points and \(q\) weights, we have \(2q\) free numbers, and with \(2q\) equations we can demand exactness for the powers from \(\xi^0\) to \(\xi^{2q-1}\). For \(q = 1\) the first equation (\(\xi^0\)) gives \(w_1 = 2\), the point is \(\xi_1 = 0\) by symmetry, and \(\xi^1\) is already satisfied. For \(q = 2\) we take the points \(\pm a\) with equal weights \(w\). For \(\xi^0\) we have \(2w = 2\), so \(w = 1\), and for \(\xi^2\) we have \(2a^2 = \tfrac23\), so \(a = 1/\sqrt3\). For \(q = 3\) we take the points \(0\) and \(\pm b\) with weights \(w_0\) and \(w_1\). For \(\xi^0\) we have \(w_0 + 2w_1 = 2\), for \(\xi^2\) we have \(2w_1 b^2 = \tfrac23\), and for \(\xi^4\) we have \(2w_1 b^4 = \tfrac25\). The quotient of the last two gives \(b^2 = \tfrac35\), then \(w_1 = \tfrac59\) and \(w_0 = \tfrac89\).

Definition 7.24 Gauss quadrature (Gaussovo pravilo)

Gauss quadrature with \(q\) points (Gaussovo pravilo s \(q\) točkami) is a rule that replaces the integral of a function \(g\) on \([-1, 1]\) by the weighted sum

\[\int_{-1}^{1} g(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi \approx \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{q} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) , \tag{7.30}\]

where \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}} \in [-1, 1]\) are points (Gauss points, Gaussove točke) and \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) are numbers (weights, uteži). For \(q = 1, 2, 3\) the points and weights are

  1. \(q = 1\): the point \(0\) with weight \(2\),
  2. \(q = 2\): the points \(\pm 1/\sqrt3\) with weights \(1\) and \(1\),
  3. \(q = 3\): the points \(0\) and \(\pm\sqrt{3/5}\) with weights \(8/9\) and \(5/9\).

Source: ONATE1 (3.40), PDF p. 113, and table 3.1, PDF p. 114, which lists the points and weights for \(q = 1, \dots, 8\) in decimal form, for example \(0{,}5773502692 = 1/\sqrt3\) and \(0{,}5555555556 = 5/9\). The derivation of the values from the equations for the powers is ours.

The rule makes sense only if it is exact for the integrands for which we chose it. The lemma says this.

Lemma 7.25 Exactness of Gauss quadrature (točnost Gaussovih pravil)

Let \(q \in \{1, 2, 3\}\). Gauss quadrature with \(q\) points (definition 7.24) gives the exact integral for every polynomial \(g\) of degree at most \(2q - 1\), \(\int_{-1}^{1} g\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}\,g(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\). For \(g = \xi^{2q}\) the sum does not give the integral.

Proof

We must show that equality holds for every power up to \(\xi^{2q-1}\), and then that it fails at \(\xi^{2q}\).

  1. By lemma 3.39, item 1, the integral is linear in \(g\), and the weighted sum is linear in \(g\) as a sum of products. Every polynomial of degree at most \(2q - 1\) is a linear combination of the powers \(1, \xi, \dots, \xi^{2q-1}\), so it suffices to check these powers.
  2. Odd powers: \(\int_{-1}^{1}\xi^m\,\mathrm{d}\xi = \big[\xi^{m+1}/(m+1)\big]_{-1}^{1} = 0\) by theorem 3.40. The points of all three rules are symmetric about \(0\) with equal weights on the pairs \(\pm\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the terms \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}^m\) and \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\,(-\xi_{\mathrm{i}})^m\) cancel and the sum is zero.
  3. Even powers, where the integral is \(2/(m+1)\). For \(q = 1\) we have \(m = 0\) and \(2 \cdot 1 = 2\). For \(q = 2\) we have \(m = 0\) and \(1 + 1 = 2\), and \(m = 2\) gives \(2 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac23\). For \(q = 3\) we have \(m = 0\) and \(\tfrac59 + \tfrac89 + \tfrac59 = 2\), \(m = 2\) and \(2 \cdot \tfrac59 \cdot \tfrac35 = \tfrac23\), and \(m = 4\) and \(2 \cdot \tfrac59 \cdot \tfrac9{25} = \tfrac25\).
  4. At the next even power the sum fails. For \(q = 1\) it is \(\xi^2\) and the sum is \(2 \cdot 0 = 0\) instead of \(\tfrac23\). For \(q = 2\) it is \(\xi^4\) and the sum is \(2 \cdot \tfrac19 = \tfrac29\) instead of \(\tfrac25\). For \(q = 3\) it is \(\xi^6\) and the sum is \(2 \cdot \tfrac59 \cdot \tfrac{27}{125} = \tfrac6{25}\) instead of \(\tfrac27\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. ONATE1, PDF p. 113: a rule of order \(q\) integrates a polynomial of degree \(2q - 1\) exactly.

The proof showed that the rules satisfy all \(2q\) equations for the powers up to \(\xi^{2q-1}\) and that at the next power they fail, as we expect, since they have only \(2q\) free numbers. For larger \(q\) the same is claimed by ONATE1 (PDF p. 113), and table 3.1 (PDF p. 114) lists the points and weights up to \(q = 8\), but no result of this chapter rests on more than three points. What this means is shown by figure 7.12: a cubic polynomial and the line through its values at the two Gauss points have the same area, because the differences above and below the line are equal in size. The line through the values \(g(\pm 1/\sqrt3)\) has area \(g(-1/\sqrt3) + g(1/\sqrt3)\), which is exactly the sum with weights \(1\) and \(1\).

We apply the rule to the element matrix. By equation (7.29), \(k_{11} = \tfrac{2EA}{h}\int_{-1}^1 (\xi - \tfrac12)^2\,\mathrm{d}\xi\), the integrand has degree 2, and by lemma 7.25 the two-point rule (\(2q - 1 = 3 \ge 2\)) is exact. The sum is \((\tfrac1{\sqrt3} - \tfrac12)^2 + (-\tfrac1{\sqrt3} - \tfrac12)^2 = 2\,(\tfrac13 + \tfrac14) = \tfrac76\), so \(k_{11} = \tfrac{2EA}{h}\cdot\tfrac76 = \tfrac{7EA}{3h}\), as in lemma 7.23. The other entries are obtained in the same way (ONATE1, example 3.3, PDF pp. 118 and 119, the same computation for \(K_{11}^{(e)}\) with two points). Three points also give the same matrix (SymPy), but it is unnecessary work.

What if we take fewer points? One point, \(\xi_1 = 0\) with weight \(2\), saves work. The strain at this point is \(u_{\mathrm{h}}' = (2/h)\,(N_1'(0)\,d_1 + N_2'(0)\,d_2 + N_3'(0)\,d_3) = (d_3 - d_1)/h\), and by equation (7.29)

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{(1)} = \frac{EA}{h} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathsf T}\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{(1)}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA}{h}\,(d_3 - d_1)^2 . \tag{7.31}\]

The energy is zero also for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (0, 1, 0)\), when only the middle node moves, although this is not a rigid shift. The field is then \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \psi_2\) (figure 7.13), the strain \(\psi_2' = (4h - 8x)/h^2\) is \(\pm 4/h\) at the ends and zero only in the middle, where the one-point rule looks at it alone. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{(1)}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), so by lemma 7.16 \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{(1)}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), and indeed the row of the middle node contains nothing. This is a spurious zero-energy mode (lažni način brez energije), also called an internal mechanism (notranji mehanizem): a motion of the element that is not rigid and that the matrix does not detect.

What does this mean for the computation? Take the hanging bar of this section with one element, but with the one-point rule. The forces of the element stay \((10{,}016, 40{,}065, 10{,}016)\) N, because we change only the integration of the stiffness. After striking out the fixed upper node the system is

\[\frac{EA}{h} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 40{,}065 \\ 10{,}016 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{N} . \tag{7.32}\]

The row of the middle node says \(0 = 40{,}065\) N: the system has no solution, because the matrix does not hold the middle node. If we left it unloaded, the system would have infinitely many solutions, since \(d_2\) would be arbitrary. One point is therefore not enough for an integrand of degree 2. We choose the number of points from the degree of the integrand, which for a quadratic element with constant stiffness means at least two, and then there is no spurious mode (lemma 7.23). ONATE1 (PDF pp. 130 and 131) warns that incomplete integration (reduced integration, nepopolno integriranje) can introduce undesirable internal mechanisms in addition to the rigid motions, that an element is stable if the stiffness matrix is integrated exactly, and that the eigenvalues must be checked on a single element and on a group of elements.

7.4.3 How fast we approach (kako hitro se približamo)

For the self weight of the hanging bar we saw that one quadratic element gives the exact field, because the true field is quadratic. This load therefore does not tell how fast the quadratic element approaches when the field is not quadratic. Take the same bar (\(L = 10\) m, \(EA = 1{,}5394 \cdot 10^7\) N, fixed at the top, free at the bottom, axis \(x\) pointing down) and the same total load \(60{,}10\) N, but distribute it linearly: zero at the top, \(q_{\mathrm{L}} = 12{,}02\) N/m at the bottom, \(q(x) = q_{\mathrm{L}}\,x/L\). This is not a physical case but a test, chosen so that the true field is not in the trial space of the quadratic element. The axial force is \(N = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q\,\mathrm{d}t = q_{\mathrm{L}}\,(L^2 - x^2)/(2L)\), and the displacement is

\[u(x) = \frac{q_{\mathrm{L}}}{2\,EA\,L}\,\Big(L^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\Big) , \tag{7.33}\]

a cubic polynomial, equal to \(26{,}03\) µm at \(x = L\) and \(17{,}89\) µm in the middle, with strain energy \(625{,}65\) µJ and \(N(0) = 60{,}10\) N.

We compare the linear and the quadratic element on meshes with \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16\) equal elements. The measure of the error is the energy of the error \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,\|u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\) (theorem 6.34), which chapter 6 used for the linear element. The values are computed with the element matrices of lemma 7.5 and lemma 7.23 and with consistent forces (SymPy and NumPy). The element matrices are assembled by theorem 7.13, whose item 3 (equality with the Ritz matrix) is proved for hat functions. Steps 4 and 5 of its proof use that the function of a node is a line on an element, determined by two values, so for quadratic elements we must replace these two steps. The function of a node is here continuous, quadratic on each element, \(1\) at its own node and \(0\) at all others, which is a shape function of the mesh (oblikovna funkcija mreže). The lemma says that on an element it equals one of the three shape functions of the element or zero.

Lemma 7.26 Shape functions of a mesh of quadratic elements (oblikovne funkcije mreže kvadratnih elementov)

Let a bar have a mesh of \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) quadratic elements, each with nodes at \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(x_{\mathrm{m}} = (x_{\mathrm{a}} + x_{\mathrm{b}})/2\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\), and let neighbouring elements share an end node. Let \(g_{\mathrm{ei}}\) be the connectivity table with \(m = 3\) columns (definition 7.10) and \(I\) the number of an unknown, that is, of a node. Then there is exactly one continuous function \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\) on the bar that is a quadratic polynomial on each element, equal to \(1\) at node \(I\) and to \(0\) at all other nodes. On element \(e\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}} = \psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\) if \(I = g_{\mathrm{ei}}\), and \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}} = 0\) if \(I\) is not in row \(e\) (the shape functions of the element \(\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\) of equation (7.24), shifted to \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\)).

Proof

We must show that a quadratic polynomial on an element is determined by its values at the three nodes, and then that the pieces assembled from these values fit together continuously.

  1. Let \(p\) be a quadratic polynomial on \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) with \(p(x_{\mathrm{a}}) = p(x_{\mathrm{m}}) = p(x_{\mathrm{b}}) = 0\). From \(p(x_{\mathrm{a}}) = 0\) we get \(p = (x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(\alpha x + \beta)\), from \(p(x_{\mathrm{b}}) = 0\) we get \(\alpha x_{\mathrm{b}} + \beta = 0\), so \(p = \alpha\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x - x_{\mathrm{b}})\), and from \(p(x_{\mathrm{m}}) = 0\) we get \(\alpha\,(x_{\mathrm{m}} - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x_{\mathrm{m}} - x_{\mathrm{b}}) = -\alpha h^2/4 = 0\) with the element length \(h = x_{\mathrm{b}} - x_{\mathrm{a}}\), so \(\alpha = 0\) and \(p = 0\).
  2. Let \(r\) be an arbitrary quadratic polynomial on the element. The polynomial \(r - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} r(x^e_{\mathrm{i}})\,\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\) is quadratic and by the definition of the shape functions has the value zero at all three nodes, so by step 1 it is zero. Every quadratic polynomial on the element is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} r(x^e_{\mathrm{i}})\,\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\), determined by its values at the nodes.
  3. By step 2, \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\) must equal \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{I}}(x^e_{\mathrm{i}})\,\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\) on element \(e\). Its values at the nodes of the element are \(1\) at node \(I\) and \(0\) at the others, so this is \(\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\) for \(I = g_{\mathrm{ei}}\) and \(0\) if \(I\) is not in row \(e\). With this \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\) is uniquely determined on each element.
  4. The \(\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\) assembled in this way is continuous. In the interior of an element it is a quadratic polynomial, at a node shared by two elements both one-sided values are the same number (\(1\) or \(0\), depending on whether this is node \(I\)), and a middle node belongs to a single element. At node \(I\) the value is \(1\) and at the others \(0\) by the definition of the shape functions.

Source: The proof is not from a source. ONATE1, figure 3.4 (PDF p. 113): assembly of the global matrix from the contributions of elements with three nodes.

With the lemma we replace steps 4 and 5 of the proof of theorem 7.13 and the remaining steps stay as they are. Step 3 needs only that the integrand is continuous on each closed element, which a polynomial is. Steps 1, 2 and 6 to 9 use only lemma 7.12, which is written for an arbitrary number \(m\) of displacements of the element, and that the field on an element is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} d^e_{\mathrm{i}}\,\psi^e_{\mathrm{i}}\), which the lemma now gives. Item 3 of the theorem therefore holds also for quadratic elements with a connectivity table of three columns, with the matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) having three rows.

element \(n\) unknowns energy of the error (µJ) quotient \(N_{\mathrm{h}}\) at the top (N) reaction (N)
linear 1 1 104,27 40,06 \(-60{,}097\)
linear 2 2 30,957 3,37 55,09 \(-60{,}097\)
linear 4 4 8,0446 3,85 58,85 \(-60{,}097\)
linear 8 8 2,0302 3,96 59,78 \(-60{,}097\)
linear 16 16 0,50876 3,99 60,02 \(-60{,}097\)
quadratic 1 2 6,5172 70,11 \(-60{,}097\)
quadratic 2 4 0,40732 16,00 62,60 \(-60{,}097\)
quadratic 4 8 0,025458 16,00 60,72 \(-60{,}097\)
quadratic 8 16 0,0015910 16,00 60,25 \(-60{,}097\)
quadratic 16 32 0,000099444 16,00 60,14 \(-60{,}097\)

The quotient is the ratio of the energy of the error at the previous mesh and at this one, that is, when \(h\) is halved. What does the table say? First, the displacements of all nodes are exact in all rows (the largest error is below \(10^{-17}\) m). For the nodes at the ends of elements this is given by theorem 6.38: the unit-force field at such a node is continuous and a line on each element, a line is a quadratic polynomial, so the field lies in the trial space of quadratic elements. For the middle nodes the theorem is silent, because the unit-force field at them has a kink in the middle of an element. That they are exact here too is said by the lemma that follows the table. Second, the energy of the error falls for the linear element with a quotient that approaches \(4 = 2^2\) (theorem 6.41 guarantees an upper bound proportional to \(h^2\), and we explain the quotient itself after the table), and for the quadratic element with a quotient \(16 = 2^4\), equal to \(16{,}00\) in all four places. Third, for the same number of unknowns the quadratic element is much better. With \(8\) unknowns the error of the linear one is \(2{,}0302\) µJ and of the quadratic one \(0{,}025458\) µJ, so about \(80\) times smaller, with \(16\) unknowns \(0{,}50876\) against \(0{,}0015910\) µJ, \(320\) times. A row of the matrix has up to five nonzero entries for the quadratic element instead of three, so there is somewhat more computation, but considerably fewer unknowns for the same accuracy. ONATE1 (PDF p. 124) says the same: the quadratic rod is better than the linear one, but for more demanding models, particularly three-dimensional ones, the improvement is offset by a more demanding mesh and a more expensive computation, so the choice is judged for each model separately. Fourth, the reaction is the same in all rows, \(-60{,}097\) N, the weight of the bar, while the axial force at the top is not: the linear element underestimates it (\(40{,}06\) against \(60{,}10\) N at \(n = 1\)), the quadratic one overestimates it (\(70{,}11\) N). The reason is the same as for the linear element in section 6.7.2. The reaction is determined by the equilibrium of the whole bar (lemma 7.20), and the axial force at the top is the derivative of the approximation at one point. The quadratic element again does not compute it exactly, although it comes closer: the error is \(+10{,}0\) N at \(n = 1\) and \(+0{,}04\) N at \(n = 16\). EP, example 8.2.1 (p. 548), notices the same for a composite bar with two quadratic elements: the force at the end, computed from the derivative of the field, is wrong by \(8{,}71\,\%\), while the force from the first equation of the system is exact.

Why exactly \(16\), and why are the middle displacements exact? For this load the true field is a cubic polynomial, so the error can be computed.

Lemma 7.27 Error of the quadratic element for a cubic field (napaka kvadratnega elementa pri kubičnem polju)

Let the bar be fixed at \(x = 0\), with axial stiffness \(EA\), constant, and let the solution of the weak form \(u\) be a cubic polynomial with third derivative \(u'''\). Let \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) be the Ritz solution in the family of continuous fields that are \(0\) at \(x = 0\) and quadratic on each of \(n\) elements of length \(h = L/n\). On each element with midpoint \(x_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(s = x - x_{\mathrm{m}}\) the error is \(u - u_{\mathrm{h}} = \tfrac16\,u'''\,s\,(s^2 - h^2/4)\). Therefore \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is exact at the midpoint of every element, and the energy of the error is \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u) = EA\,(u''')^2\,L\,h^4/1440\).

Proof

We must show that the error is a cubic polynomial that has zeros at the end points and is orthogonal to the hump of the middle node, and that this determines everything.

  1. The error \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\) on an element is the difference of a cubic and a quadratic polynomial, so a cubic polynomial with third derivative \(e''' = u'''\). At the end points of the element \(e = 0\) by theorem 6.38: the unit-force field at a node is continuous and a line on each element (the stiffness is constant), so a quadratic polynomial, and therefore it lies in the family. Let \(e = e_0 + e_1 s + e_2 s^2 + e_3 s^3\). The condition \(e(\pm h/2) = 0\) for each sign gives (the sum and the difference of the two) \(e_0 + e_2 h^2/4 = 0\) and \(e_1 + e_3 h^2/4 = 0\), so \(e = e_2\,(s^2 - h^2/4) + e_3\,s\,(s^2 - h^2/4) = (s^2 - h^2/4)(a\,s + b)\) with \(a = e_3\) and \(b = e_2\).
  2. From \(e''' = 6a\) and \(e''' = u'''\) we get \(a = u'''/6\).
  3. The shape function of the middle node, \(\psi_2 = 1 - 4s^2/h^2\) on this element and zero elsewhere, is continuous and quadratic on each element, so it is a trial field. By lemma 6.36, \(B(e, \psi_2) = EA \int e'\,\psi_2'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  4. The derivative of the error is \(e' = 3a\,s^2 + 2b\,s - a\,h^2/4\), and \(\psi_2' = -8s/h^2\). In the product the terms with \(s^3\) and \(s\) are odd and their integral over \([-h/2, h/2]\) is zero, what remains is \(\int e'\,\psi_2'\,\mathrm{d}s = -\tfrac{8}{h^2}\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} 2b\,s^2\,\mathrm{d}s = -\tfrac{8}{h^2}\cdot\tfrac{b\,h^3}{6} = -\tfrac43\,b\,h\). From step 3, \(b = 0\).
  5. With \(b = 0\) we have \(e = a\,s\,(s^2 - h^2/4)\), and at the middle \(s = 0\) we have \(e = 0\).
  6. The energy of the error on an element is \(\tfrac12\,EA\int e'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} (3s^2 - h^2/4)^2\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2\,h^5/20\) (SymPy) and \(a^2 = (u''')^2/36\), so \(EA\,(u''')^2\,h^5/1440\). Over \(n = L/h\) elements the sum is \(EA\,(u''')^2\,L\,h^4/1440\), and by theorem 6.34 this is \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u)\).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The proof showed that the error is a cubic polynomial with zeros at the end points and in the middle, whose size is determined by \(u'''\), and that the energy of the error is proportional to \(h^4\). A check: for the test load \(u''' = -q_{\mathrm{L}}/(EA\,L)\), and for \(n = 1\) the formula gives \(EA\,(u''')^2\,L\,h^4/1440 = 6{,}5172\) µJ, as in the table, and for \(n = 2\) a sixteenth of it, \(0{,}40732\) µJ. The quotient \(16\) is therefore no accident but \(h^4\), and for this load it is exact.

For the linear element we do not get the quotient \(4\) exactly (\(3{,}37\), \(3{,}85\), \(3{,}96\), \(3{,}99\)), because the energy of the error there is the sum of a term with \(h^2\) and a term with \(h^4\). We derive them. The nodal values are exact (theorem 6.38), so on an element \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{a}} + h]\) the derivative \(u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) is constant and equal to \((u(x_{\mathrm{a}} + h) - u(x_{\mathrm{a}}))/h\), which is the mean of the true derivative \(u'\) over the element (theorem 3.40). The energy of the error of an element is \(\tfrac12\,EA\int (u' - u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). For the test load \(u' = q_{\mathrm{L}}\,(L^2 - x^2)/(2\,EA\,L)\) is a quadratic polynomial, and SymPy gives \(h^3 q_{\mathrm{L}}^2\,(4h^2 + 15\,h\,x_{\mathrm{a}} + 15\,x_{\mathrm{a}}^2)/(360\,EA\,L^2)\) for this integral. The sum over the elements \(x_{\mathrm{a}} = 0, h, \dots, (n-1)h\) with \(nh = L\) is

\[\begin{aligned} \Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u) &= \frac{q_{\mathrm{L}}^2\,L}{72\,EA}\,h^2 - \frac{q_{\mathrm{L}}^2}{360\,EA\,L}\,h^4 \\ &= 1{,}3034\,h^2 - 0{,}002607\,h^4\ \text{µJ} , \end{aligned} \tag{7.34}\]

where \(h\) is in metres. The values in the table agree in all the digits written (at \(n = 1\), \(130{,}34 - 26{,}07 = 104{,}27\) µJ). Since the second term falls faster, the quotient approaches \(4\) as \(h\) is reduced.

For a general smooth field, however, this book does not prove the law \(h^4\) for quadratic elements. It is claimed by BATHE in section 4.3.5 (PDF pp. 263 to 265): for elements with polynomials of degree \(k\) the error in the energy norm (4.101) is proportional to \(h^k\), so the energy to \(h^{2k}\), for \(k = 2\) to \(h^4\). BATHE states the estimate of the interpolation error (4.100), on which this rests, as a known result of interpolation theory without a proof, and compares the measured order \(3{,}91\) with the theoretical \(4\) (PDF p. 265). This book has an interpolation estimate only for a line (lemma 6.40), so the law \(h^4\) is here proved for the cubic field (lemma 7.27) and for the quartic field that follows it is supported by computation.

Is the midpoint exact also for a field that is not a cubic polynomial? A check with a polynomial of degree four, again with quadratic elements: the load \(q = 3q_0\,(x/L)^2\) (\(q_0 = 6{,}0097\) N/m, in total again \(q_0 L = 60{,}10\) N) gives an end displacement of \(29{,}28\) µm, which is exact for all \(n\). The errors at the middle of the first element are, however, \(0{,}122\) µm (\(n = 1\)), \(0{,}00762\) µm (\(n = 2\)) and \(0{,}000477\) µm (\(n = 4\)), so they are not zero, and they fall with the quotient \(16\) (SymPy). The exactness of the midpoint is therefore a property of cubic fields, in which the error on an element is by the lemma odd about the middle of the element, not a property of the element. Figure 7.14 shows the difference for the same number of unknowns.

The figure shows the same content as the table. For one quadratic element and two linear ones the unknowns are the same, and the error is almost three times smaller (the largest \(0{,}63\) against \(1{,}84\) µm), and the energy of the error \(4{,}75\) times (\(6{,}5172\) against \(30{,}957\) µJ). With more elements the difference grows: with each halving the energy of the linear one is reduced by \(4\) and of the quadratic one by \(16\) (figure 7.15).

For a load that varies along the bar, the quadratic element therefore gives, for the same number of unknowns, an error that is \(80\) times smaller with \(8\) unknowns and \(320\) times smaller with \(16\). For the truss in section 7.5, where the loads are only at the nodes, the true axial force in each bar is constant, so one linear element per bar suffices and the quadratic element brings no improvement.

7.5 The plane truss (paličje v ravnini)

So far we have written the matrix of a bar for displacements along the bar, one number per node (section 7.1.2). In a truss the bars point in different directions and the nodes move in the plane, each with two numbers. What does the matrix of one bar look like in the axes of the whole truss? And if we know it, can we compute the truss of chapters 4 and 5 by the same procedure as any other, even one with a hundred bars? In this section we write the matrix of a bar in an arbitrary direction and with it compute the wall truss of chapter 4 for the fifth time. Then we look at when the matrix of the structure is not invertible, because the truss is not supported enough or moves without any bar stretching.

The model is the truss of definition 4.4: straight bars connected by pins, forces only at the nodes, the weight of the bars negligible. Every bar has a constant \(EA\) and is one finite element (definition 7.1) with two nodes. The displacements are small, and we write the matrix of the structure on the shape before loading, as in chapter 4. The displacement of node \(i\) in the axes \(x\) and \(y\) of the whole truss (the global axes, globalne osi) is denoted by the column \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = (u_{\mathrm{i}}, v_{\mathrm{i}})\).

7.5.1 Local and global axes (lokalne in globalne osi)

Let the bar go from node \(i\) to node \(j\), with the nodes at the coordinates \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{j}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\). The length of the bar is \(L = \sqrt{(x_{\mathrm{j}} - x_{\mathrm{i}})^2 + (y_{\mathrm{j}} - y_{\mathrm{i}})^2}\) and the unit vector from \(i\) towards \(j\) is

\[\vek n = (c, s) = \Big(\frac{x_{\mathrm{j}} - x_{\mathrm{i}}}{L},\ \frac{y_{\mathrm{j}} - y_{\mathrm{i}}}{L}\Big) .\]

The numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are the cosine and the sine of the angle between the bar and the axis \(x\), so they form the first row of the rotation matrix (definition 2.37) when the new axis \(\bar x\) lies along the bar (figure 7.16).

The \(2 \times 2\) matrix of lemma 7.5 holds for the displacements \(\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\bar u_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the ends along the bar. Which numbers are these if we know the displacements \(\vek u_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the global axes? By section 4.4.9, when an end moves, the bar is lengthened by the projection of the displacement on the direction of the bar, \(\vek n\cdot\vek u\), while the part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar only turns it (equation (4.48)). The same holds when both ends move. The vector of the bar is then \(L\,\vek n + \vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the derivation of section 4.4.9, in which the difference of the end displacements stands in place of the displacement of the node, gives the elongation \(\vek n\cdot(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}})\) up to a neglected term, the square of the length of the difference of the displacements divided by \(2L\). This term is small when the displacements of the ends are much smaller than the length \(L\) of the bar. For the bar \(BC\) of the wall truss (\(L = 5\) m), when \(C\) moves 1 mm downwards, the elongation to first order is \(0{,}6\) mm, and the exact computation gives \(0{,}600064\) mm. Hence the displacement of an end along the bar is the projection

\[\bar u_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{i}} = c\,u_{\mathrm{i}} + s\,v_{\mathrm{i}} , \qquad \bar u_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} = c\,u_{\mathrm{j}} + s\,v_{\mathrm{j}} .\]

We put them into a column of four numbers \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (u_{\mathrm{i}}, v_{\mathrm{i}}, u_{\mathrm{j}}, v_{\mathrm{j}})\), the displacements of the ends of the bar in the global axes. The numbers \(\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\bar u_{\mathrm{j}}\) are obtained from it by the \(2 \times 4\) matrix

\[\mat T_{\mathrm{e}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vek n^\T & \vek 0^\T \\ \vek 0^\T & \vek n^\T \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c & s & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c & s \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{pmatrix} \bar u_{\mathrm{i}} \\ \bar u_{\mathrm{j}} \end{pmatrix} = \mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} .\]

The matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\) takes a column of four numbers and returns a column of two.

How does the matrix of the bar depend on these four numbers? A lemma connects the energy of the bar with the global displacements.

Lemma 7.28 Stiffness matrix of a bar in global axes (togostna matrika palice v globalnih oseh)

Let a straight bar with ends \(i\) and \(j\) have length \(L > 0\) and a constant \(EA > 0\), and let \(\vek n\) be the unit vector from \(i\) towards \(j\) in the global axes. Let the displacements of the ends be small, let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (\vek u_{\mathrm{i}}, \vek u_{\mathrm{j}})\) be the column of the displacements of the ends in the global axes and \(\bar{\mat k} = \frac{EA}{L}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) the matrix of lemma 7.5. Then the strain energy of the bar is \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), the forces of the surroundings on the ends of the bar, put into a column \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\), are \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), with the symmetric matrix

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\bar{\mat k}\,\mat T_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA}{L}\begin{bmatrix} \vek n\,\vek n^\T & -\vek n\,\vek n^\T \\ -\vek n\,\vek n^\T & \vek n\,\vek n^\T \end{bmatrix} , \tag{7.35}\]

that is, the stiffness matrix of the bar (definition 7.4) in the global axes. In the plane \(\vek n\,\vek n^\T = \begin{bmatrix} c^2 & cs \\ cs & s^2 \end{bmatrix}\). The same formula holds in space, where \(\vek n\) has three components, \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\) is of size \(2 \times 6\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) of size \(6 \times 6\).

Proof

We must show that the energy in global displacements is a quadratic form with the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\bar{\mat k}\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\), that this matrix is a product of a column and a row with blocks \(\pm\vek n\,\vek n^\T\), and that the same product gives the forces on the ends from the displacements of the ends, which is the definition of a stiffness matrix.

  1. By equation (4.48), used for both ends, the elongation of the bar is \(e = \vek n\cdot(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}}) = \bar u_{\mathrm{j}} - \bar u_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \((\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}, \bar u_{\mathrm{j}}) = \mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. By lemma 4.5 the bar has a constant axial force \(N = EA\,e/L\), so by equation (4.5) \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = N^2 L/(2EA) = \tfrac12\,\frac{EA}{L}\,e^2\).
  3. The matrix \(\bar{\mat k}\) gives \((\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}, \bar u_{\mathrm{j}})\,\bar{\mat k}\,(\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}, \bar u_{\mathrm{j}})^\T = \frac{EA}{L}\,(\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2\,\bar u_{\mathrm{i}}\bar u_{\mathrm{j}} + \bar u_{\mathrm{j}}^2) = \frac{EA}{L}\,e^2\). Hence \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}})^\T\bar{\mat k}\,(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}})\).
  4. By lemma 1.101 on the transpose of a product, \((\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}})^\T = \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\), so \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\bar{\mat k}\,\mat T_{\mathrm{e}})\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). The matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\bar{\mat k}\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric, because \(\bar{\mat k}\) is symmetric and transposing a product reverses the order of the factors.
  5. Write \(\bar{\mat k} = \frac{EA}{L}\,\vek a\,\vek a^\T\) with \(\vek a = (1, -1)\) (a column). The transposed matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\) has size \(4 \times 2\) and \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek a = (\vek n, -\vek n)\), a column with four components.
