By point 3 of the lemma the mirror bar has the same force \(N\) and the same component \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) (reflection in the vertical does not change the component \(y\)), so the contribution is equal. The row is thus equal to \(2 \times\) (contribution of the left bars) \(+\) the contribution of \(b_3t_3\) with the full cross-section \(= f_{\mathrm{y}}(b_3) = -10\) kN. Halved, this is the row of the model \(H\): (contribution of the left bars) \(+\) the contribution of \(b_3t_3\) with the cross-section \(A/2\) \(= -5\) kN. The same holds for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) at \(t_3\) (the load there is zero).
  4. The rows \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) at \(b_3\) and \(t_3\) in the model \(H\) are not equations, because these unknowns are prescribed, and their values are reactions.
  5. So \(\tilde{\vek d}\) satisfies all equations of the model \(H\). The matrix of the model \(H\) is positive definite (all \(11\) pivots are positive, the smallest is \(2{,}14 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, computed in NumPy), so the system has exactly one solution (theorem 6.29), and this is \(\tilde{\vek d}\). The axial forces and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of the full model are therefore equal in \(H\).

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): "Load on this octant is Px/2, because the original load Px is bisected by the symmetry plane" and "only half its stiffness is retained in the portion analyzed". The proof is not from the source.

The support at \(b_0\) is thus a roller in the half model, not a fixed support. The model \(H\) gives \(11\) unknowns instead of \(21\), all axial forces of the full model, the displacement of the middle \(7{,}305\) mm and the reactions on the cut \(+45\) kN at \(b_3\) and \(-45\) kN at \(t_3\). These are the horizontal forces with which the other half acts on this half. At \(b_3\) this is the force of the bottom chord \(40\) kN and the horizontal component of the diagonal \(t_4b_3\), \(7{,}071 \cdot \cos 45^\circ = 5\) kN, and at \(t_3\) the force of the top chord \(-45\) kN. Together they form a couple with the moment \(45 \cdot 3 = 135\) kN m, which is the bending moment of the bridge in the middle, \(25 \cdot 9 - 10\,(6 + 3) = 135\) kN m.

What happens if at \(b_0\) instead of the roller support we prescribe also \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(b_0) = 0\), because the bridge is in reality fixed on this side? We compute with the model \(H^*\): the same as \(H\), only with a fixed support at \(b_0\) (figure 7.29). The solution has \(10\) free unknowns. The axial force of the bar \(b_0b_1\) is \(-5\) kN instead of \(25\) kN, of the bar \(b_1b_2\) \(-5\) kN instead of \(25\) kN and of the bar \(b_2b_3\) \(10\) kN instead of \(40\) kN, and the sag of the middle is \(5{,}469\) mm instead of \(7{,}305\) mm. The reaction at \(b_0\) is \((30, 25)\) kN, at \(b_3\) the horizontal one is \(15\) kN and at \(t_3\) the horizontal one is \(-45\) kN. We check the equilibrium of the reactions: \(\sum F_{\mathrm{x}} = 30 + 15 - 45 = 0\), \(\sum F_{\mathrm{y}} = 25 - 10 - 10 - 5 = 0\) and the moment about \(b_0\) is \(-(10 \cdot 3 + 10 \cdot 6 + 5 \cdot 9) + 45 \cdot 3 = -135 + 135 = 0\). The check of the reactions succeeds, but the model is wrong.

Why does the check of the reactions not catch the error? Lemma 7.30 says that the reactions balance the load for every solution of the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\), because \(\mat K\,\vek d_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\) for every rigid motion (step 3 of lemma 7.30). This holds also for a model with wrong supports, since this is again a correctly solved problem, only a different problem. The correct solution has \(\tilde u_{\mathrm{x}}(b_0) = -c/2 = -1{,}378\) mm: the end of the bottom chord must move so that the chord can stretch. The model \(H^*\) forbids this, since it holds the joints \(b_0\) and \(b_3\), which are \(9\) m apart, in place horizontally. The chord cannot stretch, the forces in it change, the half of the bridge is supported too stiffly and the sag is too small by a quarter. The check of the reactions is necessary, not sufficient.

Other checks catch the error. The first is the horizontal reaction: lemma 7.38 says that the horizontal reaction at \(b_0\) is zero in the full model, while the model \(H^*\) gives \(30\) kN. The second is the computation with a section: the force in the bottom chord \(b_2b_3\) is \(40\) kN (step 2 of the check with a section above), while the model \(H^*\) gives \(10\) kN. The third is a comparison of the half model with the full one: the displacement of the middle must be the same, \(7{,}305\) mm. None of the three needs new knowledge about the bridge, they only require that we compare the written computation with what we know from equilibrium.

7.8 Mathematics: sparse and banded matrices (redke in pasovne matrike)

The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of the bridge from section 7.7 has order \(21\), so \(21 \cdot 21 = 441\) entries, of which only \(93\) are nonzero, that is \(21\,\%\). Almost four fifths, exactly \(348\) entries or \(78{,}9\,\%\), are zeros, and the nonzero entries lie near the main diagonal (figure 7.30). This raises two questions. May we leave the zeros out of the computation, and how much do we save? And does the elimination of chapter 6 (theorem 6.29) keep the zeros, or fill them with nonzero numbers? This section is mathematical: it proves statements about matrices, and for the bridge each one is tested with numbers.

7.8.1 Sparse and banded matrix (redka in pasovna matrika)

A matrix is sparse (redka matrika) if most of its entries are zero (COOK, PDF p. 51, "Sparsity": "A matrix is called sparse if it contains many zeros"). For practical structures with hundreds or thousands of elements, more than \(99\,\%\) of the entries of the stiffness matrix may be zero by the same source, so programs use special storage formats and algorithms. Why the matrix of the bridge is sparse too, corollary 7.14 tells us, which holds for every structure made of elements, so also for the truss of section 7.5: the entry \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is zero if the unknowns \(i\) and \(j\) are not at nodes of the same element. A bar connects only the nodes at its two ends, and at most five bars meet at any node of the bridge. So no row of the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) has more than \(7\) nonzero entries (by counting), and this would stay so for a bridge with more bays, because the number of bars at a node would not grow. The number of nonzero entries would therefore grow in proportion to the order \(n\) of the matrix, and the number of all entries as the square \(n^2\).

Where in a row are the nonzero entries? For the hanging bar of chapter 6 we numbered the nodes of the bar in order and only three diagonals were nonzero, as the matrix (6.15) shows. For the bridge the answer depends on how we numbered the unknowns, and that numbering is our choice. How far from the diagonal the nonzero entries reach, we capture with one number.

Definition 7.40 Banded matrix (pasovna matrika)

Let \(\mat K\) be a square matrix of order \(n\) with entries \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and let \(b\) be an integer between \(0\) and \(n - 1\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is banded (pasovna) with half-bandwidth (polovična širina pasu) \(b\) if

\[K_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0 \quad \text{for every pair } (i, j) \text{ with } |i - j| > b . \tag{7.39}\]

The nonzero entries therefore lie in the band between the diagonals \(j = i - b\) and \(j = i + b\). The half-bandwidth of a matrix is the smallest such number \(b\).

Source: COOK, PDF p. 58, "semibandwidth": for row \(i\) it is the number of columns from the diagonal to the rightmost nonzero entry, and for the whole matrix the source takes the root-mean-square average over the rows. We take the largest distance \(|i - j|\) that carries a nonzero entry, so that the band certainly contains all nonzero entries. The source counts the diagonal in a row, we do not.

For the matrix (6.15) we have \(b = 1\). A banded matrix with \(b = 0\) is diagonal. If \(b = n - 1\), the condition (7.39) demands nothing and every matrix is banded, but the band is worth nothing.

For a truss we number by nodes, as in the paragraph on unknowns in section 7.5: we number the nodes \(1, \dots, N\), every node has \(r\) unknowns (\(r = 1\) for the bar, \(r = 2\) for the plane truss and \(r = 3\) for the space truss), and the unknowns of node \(p\) get the numbers \(r(p - 1) + 1, \dots, rp\). For the plane truss these are \(2p - 1\) and \(2p\). The band of the matrix is then decided by one datum, namely how far apart the numbers of the nodes of one element are.

Lemma 7.41 Band of the structure matrix (pas matrike konstrukcije)

Let a mesh have \(N\) nodes numbered \(1, \dots, N\), and let every node have \(r\) unknowns, numbered by nodes (node \(p\) has the unknowns \(r(p - 1) + 1, \dots, rp\)). Let \(m\) be the largest difference \(|p - q|\) of the numbers of two nodes that belong to the same element. Then the structure matrix \(\mat K\) has half-bandwidth

\[b \le r\,(m + 1) - 1 . \tag{7.40}\]

The matrix of free unknowns \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\), obtained by deleting the rows and columns of the prescribed unknowns (theorem 7.18), has half-bandwidth at most as large.

Proof

We must show that \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for \(|i - j| > r(m + 1) - 1\). We assume \(i \le j\), which loses no generality because of the symmetry of the matrix 7.14.

  1. Let \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} \ne 0\). By corollary 7.14 the unknowns \(i\) and \(j\) stand in the same row of the connectivity table, that is in the same element, so they are at nodes \(p\) and \(q\) of this element (\(p = q\) is allowed).
  2. Since \(i \le j\), we have \(p \le q\), because the unknowns are numbered by nodes. By the definition of \(m\), \(q - p \le m\).
  3. For the unknown \(i\) of node \(p\) we have \(i \ge r(p - 1) + 1\), and for the unknown \(j\) of node \(q\) we have \(j \le rq\).
  4. Therefore \(j - i \le rq - r(p - 1) - 1 = r(q - p + 1) - 1 \le r(m + 1) - 1\). This is (7.40).
  5. For \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) we delete the rows and columns of some unknowns, and the remaining ones keep their order. The new number of an unknown is the old one decreased by the number of deleted unknowns before it, so the difference of the numbers of two remaining unknowns does not grow. The same bound therefore holds for \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. COOK, PDF p. 51 ("Sparsity") and EP, p. 541 for the condition that \(K_{\mathrm{IJ}}\) is zero if the nodes are not in the same element.

Let us test it on the hanging bar: \(r = 1\), nodes in order and \(m = 1\) give \(b \le 1 \cdot 2 - 1 = 1\), the tridiagonal matrix (6.15). Now let us look at two numberings of the bridge (figure 7.30), with the node names from section 7.7.1 (\(b_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the bottom, \(t_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the top chord of the bridge). A chord (pas mostu) is the row of bars along the bottom or top edge of the bridge, the band of a matrix (pas matrike) the places next to the diagonal of definition 7.40, and the two meanings must not be confused, since Slovenian uses the same word for both. In the first we go along the span: \(b_0, b_1, t_1, b_2, t_2, \dots, b_5, t_5, b_6\) get the numbers \(1\) to \(12\). In the second we number the nodes of the bottom chord first, \(b_0, \dots, b_6\) with \(1\) to \(7\), and then those of the top chord, \(t_1, \dots, t_5\) with \(8\) to \(12\), and we call this the numbering by rows.

  1. Along the span, the farthest apart are the bar \(t_4 b_3\) between the numbers \(9\) and \(6\) and the bar \(t_5 b_4\) between \(11\) and \(8\), so \(m = 3\) and \(b \le 2 \cdot 4 - 1 = 7\). The computation gives \(b = 7\) for \(\mat K\) and for \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\), so the bound is reached.
  2. By rows, the farthest apart are the bar \(b_0 t_1\) between \(1\) and \(8\) and the bar \(t_4 b_3\) between \(11\) and \(4\), so \(m = 7\) and \(b \le 2 \cdot 8 - 1 = 15\). The matrix \(\mat K\) has \(b = 15\) indeed, but the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) has \(b = 14\), because between the unknown \(u\) of node \(b_3\) and the unknown \(v\) of node \(t_4\) the unknown \(v\) of node \(b_6\) (a support) is deleted, so the numbers come closer by \(1\).

The cause of the difference is simple. A bar of the bridge reaches at most across one bay, and in the numbering along the span every bay adds only two numbers (\(b_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{i}}\)), so the two nodes of one bar have numbers at most \(3\) apart. In the numbering by rows the vertical bar \(b_{\mathrm{i}} t_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the numbers \(i + 1\) and \(i + 7\), always \(6\) apart, because the bottom chord has \(7\) nodes. The bars \(b_0 t_1\), \(t_4 b_3\) and \(t_5 b_4\) are \(7\) apart. A longer bridge would have the same \(b\) in the first numbering, but in the second \(b\) would grow with the length of the bridge. The number of nonzero entries is the same in both cases, \(93\), since the matrices are the same, only the unknowns are in another order.

7.8.2 Elimination keeps the band (eliminacija ohrani pas)

Zeros and band count only if the elimination does not destroy them. Let us repeat one step of elimination from the proof of theorem 6.29. We write the matrix as \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} K_{11} & \vek g^\T \\ \vek g & \mat K' \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), where \(\vek g\) is the column of entries \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = K_{\mathrm{i}1}\) for \(i = 2, \dots, n\) (in chapter 6 this column is called \(\vek b\), here we write \(\vek g\) so that the letter \(b\) remains the half-bandwidth). After the step the matrix \(\mat K'' = \mat K' - \vek g\,\vek g^\T/K_{11}\) remains, with entries

\[K''_{\mathrm{ij}} = K_{\mathrm{ij}} - \frac{g_{\mathrm{i}}\,g_{\mathrm{j}}}{K_{11}} \qquad (i, j = 2, \dots, n) . \tag{7.41}\]

The entry \((i, j)\) therefore changes only if \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{j}}\) are both nonzero. If \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) but \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{j}}\) are nonzero, the entry becomes nonzero. This is called fill (zapolnitev): a zero that the elimination turns into a nonzero number (COOK, PDF p. 57: "a direct (noniterative) equation solver creates fills").

For the hanging bar \(\vek g\) has only one nonzero entry, so the elimination changes only one diagonal entry and there is no fill. For the bridge with the numbering along the span (the unknowns \(1, 2, \dots, 6\) are \(u\) and \(v\) of the nodes \(b_1\), \(t_1\) and \(b_2\), the unknown \(7\) is \(u\) of node \(t_2\)) it is so in the first two steps. The third step has the pivot \(K_{33}\), which is the unknown \(u\) of node \(t_1\). Its column has nonzero entries in the rows \(5\), \(6\) and \(7\), because \(t_1\) is connected to node \(b_2\) by an oblique bar (it links \(u\) of node \(t_1\) with \(u\) and \(v\) of node \(b_2\)) and to node \(t_2\) by a horizontal bar (it links \(u\) with \(u\)). The entry \(K_{43}\), which links \(u\) and \(v\) of node \(t_1\), is zero, because the contributions of the oblique bars \(b_0 t_1\) and \(t_1 b_2\) cancel in it: the bars have the same \(EA/L\) and the product of direction cosines \(cs = +\tfrac12\) and \(-\tfrac12\). By equation (7.41) all entries with three rows and columns \(5, 6, 7\) change, also the entries \((7, 5)\) and \((7, 6)\), which were zero, since the nodes \(b_2\) and \(t_2\) are connected only by a vertical bar, and that links only \(v\) with \(v\). The elimination of the unknown \(u\) of node \(t_1\) expresses it by the unknowns of its neighbours and so links them to each other. Whether the band endures this, the next lemma tells.

Lemma 7.42 Elimination keeps the band (eliminacija ohrani pas)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\) with half-bandwidth \(b\). Let \(\mat K^{(1)} = \mat K\) and let \(\mat K^{(k+1)}\) be the matrix that remains after the \(k\)-th step of elimination without row exchanges (the matrix \(\mat K''\) of equation (7.41) for \(\mat K^{(k)}\)), of order \(n - k\). Then every matrix \(\mat K^{(k)}\) is symmetric, positive definite and has half-bandwidth at most \(b\). Entries outside the band therefore stay zero throughout the elimination, and fill occurs only inside the band.

Proof

We prove it by induction on \(k\) (theorem 1.44). The statement \(P(k)\): the matrix \(\mat K^{(k)}\) is symmetric, positive definite and \(K^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for \(|i - j| > b\).

  1. Start. \(P(1)\) holds by assumption.
  2. Induction step. Let \(P(k)\) hold for some \(k < n\) and let \(\mat K^{(k)}\) be written as above with \(K_{11}\), \(\vek g\) and \(\mat K'\). By theorem 6.29, steps 5 and 6 of the proof, \(\mat K^{(k+1)} = \mat K^{(k)\prime\prime}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
  3. The entry \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = K_{\mathrm{i}1}\) is zero for \(i > b + 1\), because \(|i - 1| = i - 1 > b\) and \(K_{\mathrm{i}1} = 0\) by \(P(k)\).
  4. Let \(|i - j| > b\) with \(i, j \ge 2\). If \(i\) and \(j\) were both at most \(b + 1\), they would lie in \(2, \dots, b + 1\) and the difference would be \(|i - j| \le b - 1\). Hence at least one of the numbers \(i\), \(j\) is greater than \(b + 1\), and by step 3 at least one of \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(g_{\mathrm{j}}\) is zero.
  5. By equation (7.41), then, \(K''_{\mathrm{ij}} = K_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{j}}/K_{11} = 0 - 0 = 0\), since \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) by \(P(k)\). The matrix \(\mat K^{(k+1)}\) is therefore banded with half-bandwidth at most \(b\) (the difference of two row numbers does not change, because the rows \(2, \dots, n\) get the numbers \(1, \dots, n - 1\), all decreased by \(1\)). This is \(P(k + 1)\).
  6. By the principle of induction \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k = 1, \dots, n\) (the matrix \(\mat K^{(n)}\) has order \(1\)).

Source: The proof is not from a source. COOK, PDF p. 58: for a matrix with a small profile there is little fill in the elimination, "Then nonzero entries in the structure matrix are tightly clustered along its diagonal, so elimination produces few fills".

The lemma says that there is no fill outside the band. How much of it there is inside the band it does not say, so we count on the bridge. The lower triangle of the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) has \(57\) nonzero entries in both numberings (\(21\) on the diagonal and \(36\) below it). After the elimination, the lower triangle of multipliers, which we will call \(\mat L\) in the next section, has \(83\) nonzero entries in the numbering along the span, so the fill is \(83 - 57 = 26\) entries. In the numbering by rows it has \(121\) and the fill is \(121 - 57 = 64\) (figure 7.31). A wider band leaves more room for fill: below the diagonal and including it, the band holds \(140\) entries for \(b = 7\) and \(210\) for \(b = 14\), of \(231\) in the lower triangle altogether.

How much work do we save? We count work as the number of multiplications and divisions. For counting we need the sum \(1^2 + 2^2 + \dots + m^2\), which section 3.5 wrote without proof in the history box on Cavalieri. We prove it now, by induction.

Lemma 7.43 Sum of the squares of natural numbers (vsota kvadratov naravnih števil)

For every natural number \(m\)

\[\begin{aligned} 1 + 2 + \dots + m &= \frac{m\,(m + 1)}{2} , \\ 1^2 + 2^2 + \dots + m^2 &= \frac{m\,(m + 1)(2m + 1)}{6} . \end{aligned} \tag{7.42}\]
Proof

We prove it by induction on \(m\) (theorem 1.44) for both equalities together.

  1. Start, \(m = 1\). The left side of both is \(1\), the right sides are \(1 \cdot 2/2 = 1\) and \(1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3/6 = 1\).
  2. Induction step. Let the equalities hold for \(m\). To the first sum we add \(m + 1\), to the second \((m + 1)^2\).
  3. The first sum becomes \(\frac{m(m + 1)}{2} + (m + 1) = \frac{(m + 1)(m + 2)}{2}\). This is the first equality for \(m + 1\).
  4. The second sum becomes \(\frac{m(m + 1)(2m + 1)}{6} + (m + 1)^2 = \frac{(m + 1)\,\big(m(2m + 1) + 6(m + 1)\big)}{6} = \frac{(m + 1)(2m^2 + 7m + 6)}{6}\).
  5. Since \((m + 2)(2m + 3) = 2m^2 + 7m + 6\), this is \(\frac{(m + 1)(m + 2)(2m + 3)}{6}\), which is the second equality for \(m + 1\), because \(2(m + 1) + 1 = 2m + 3\).
  6. By the principle of induction the equalities hold for every \(m\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The equality is stated without proof in section 3.5.

The proof showed that the formula holds for every \(m\), because it holds for \(m = 1\) and passes from \(m\) to \(m + 1\).

Lemma 7.44 Cost of elimination (cena eliminacije)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\). Elimination without row exchanges that uses the symmetry and corrects only the lower triangle in every step performs, for a full matrix,

\[\frac{(n - 1)\,n\,(n + 1)}{6} \approx \frac{n^3}{6} \tag{7.43}\]

multiplications in the corrections of entries and \(n(n - 1)/2\) divisions in the computation of the multipliers. If \(\mat K\) has half-bandwidth \(b < n\) and in every step we skip the rows that have a zero in the pivot column, the number of multiplications is at most

\[\frac{b\,(b + 1)\,(3n - 2b - 1)}{6} \approx \frac{n\,b^2}{2} \quad (n \gg b \gg 1) , \tag{7.44}\]

and the number of divisions at most \(b\,(2n - b - 1)/2 \approx n\,b\). The bounds are reached if in every step all \(b\) entries below the pivot are nonzero.

Proof

We must show that the number of operations is as stated. We count step by step. Let \(k = 1, \dots, n - 1\) be the step in which the matrix \(\mat K^{(k)}\) has order \(n - k + 1\) (notation of lemma 7.42).

  1. In step \(k\) there are \(s = n - k\) rows below the pivot. The multiplier of row \(i\) is \(g_{\mathrm{i}}/K_{11}\), which is one division per row, \(s\) divisions in all.
  2. The correction \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{j}}/K_{11} = K_{\mathrm{ij}} - \ell_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the already computed multiplier \(\ell_{\mathrm{i}} = g_{\mathrm{i}}/K_{11}\) is one multiplication. Since the matrix is symmetric (step 5 of the proof of theorem 6.29), we correct only the entries \((i, j)\) with \(i \ge j\) among the \(s\) rows, that is \(s(s + 1)/2\) entries and as many multiplications.
  3. For a full matrix the sum over the steps, as \(s = n - k\) goes from \(1\) to \(n - 1\), by lemma 7.43 with \(m = n - 1\) is
    \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{n-1} \frac{s(s + 1)}{2} &= \frac12\left(\frac{(n - 1)\,n\,(2n - 1)}{6} + \frac{(n - 1)\,n}{2}\right) \\ &= \frac{(n - 1)\,n\,\big((2n - 1) + 3\big)}{12} = \frac{(n - 1)\,n\,(n + 1)}{6} . \end{aligned}\]
    The number of divisions is \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{n-1} s = n(n - 1)/2\). This is (7.43).
  4. For a banded matrix, by lemma 7.42 all entries outside the band of every matrix \(\mat K^{(k)}\) are zero, so in step \(k\) only \(t_{\mathrm{k}} = \min(b, n - k)\) entries of the column \(\vek g\) are nonzero (step 3 of the proof of the lemma). Multipliers and corrections are needed only for these rows, so at most \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\) divisions and \(t_{\mathrm{k}}(t_{\mathrm{k}} + 1)/2\) multiplications (exactly as many if all these entries are really nonzero).
  5. For \(k \le n - b\) we have \(t_{\mathrm{k}} = b\), and for \(k > n - b\) the number \(t_{\mathrm{k}} = n - k\) goes from \(b - 1\) to \(1\). The sum of these upper bounds is
    \[\begin{aligned} (n - b)\,\frac{b(b + 1)}{2} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^{b-1}\frac{s(s + 1)}{2} &= (n - b)\,\frac{b(b + 1)}{2} + \frac{(b - 1)\,b\,(b + 1)}{6} \\ &= \frac{b(b + 1)}{6}\,\big(3(n - b) + (b - 1)\big) , \end{aligned}\]
    where we computed the second sum as in step 3 with \(b - 1\) instead of \(n - 1\). The bracket is \(3n - 2b - 1\), which is (7.44). The number of divisions is \((n - b)\,b + b(b - 1)/2 = b\,(2n - b - 1)/2\).
  6. For \(n \gg b \gg 1\) we have \(b + 1 \approx b\) and \(3n - 2b - 1 \approx 3n\), so \(b \cdot b \cdot 3n/6 = n b^2/2\).

Source: The counting is not from a source. The same proportionality \(n^3\) for a full matrix is given by KREYSZIG, PDF p. 876 (crop p876-b2): \(f(n) = \tfrac12 (n - 1) n + \tfrac23 (n^2 - 1) n \approx \tfrac23 n^3\), where the source counts divisions, multiplications and subtractions for a nonsymmetric matrix, so \(\tfrac13 n^3\) multiplications. COOK, PDF p. 58: for a matrix with \(n \gg b\) the computational effort is "approximately proportional to \(nb^2\)".

The lemma and its bound for \(n \gg b\) say that the cost grows only linearly with the order \(n\) if the band stays equally wide, and for a full matrix as the third power. For the bridge with \(n = 21\) unknowns:

  1. Full matrix: by equation (7.43), \(20 \cdot 21 \cdot 22/6 = 1540\) multiplications and \(210\) divisions, \(1750\) operations in all.
  2. Band \(b = 7\) (along the span), all entries of the band: by equation (7.44), \(7 \cdot 8 \cdot (63 - 15)/6 = 448\) multiplications and \(7 \cdot (42 - 8)/2 = 119\) divisions, at most \(567\) in all. If in every step we count only the entries that are really nonzero in that step (including the fill created earlier), the number of operations is \(148 + 62 = 210\).
  3. Band \(b = 14\) (by rows), all entries of the band give at most \(1190\) multiplications, which is almost as many as for the full matrix, and \(189\) divisions, \(1379\) in all. Skipping zeros, it is \(380 + 100 = 480\) operations.

The approximation \(n b^2/2\) would give \(21 \cdot 196/2 = 2058\) for \(b = 14\), which is more than the full cost \(1540\). This is no contradiction: the approximation \(n b^2/2\) holds for \(n \gg b\), and for the bridge \(b = 14\) is only a little less than \(n = 21\), and the exact equation (7.44) gives \(1190 < 1540\). The order \(21\) is too small for the band to save much, so let us look at a larger system. A mesh of \(50 \times 100\) nodes with two unknowns per node has \(n = 10^4\) unknowns. If we number the nodes by rows of length \(50\) and every element also connects diagonally neighbouring nodes, then \(m = 51\) and by equation (7.40) \(b \le 2 \cdot 52 - 1 = 103\), which for an estimate we round to \(b = 100\) (an example for an estimate, not the computation of some structure, with \(b = 103\) it would be \(5{,}3 \cdot 10^7\)). For \(n = 10^4\) and \(b = 100\) such a system needs \(n^3/6 = 1{,}7 \cdot 10^{11}\) multiplications for a full matrix and \(n b^2/2 = 5 \cdot 10^7\) for a banded one, which is \(3300\) times fewer. For \(n = 10^6\) and \(b = 10^3\) the ratio is \(3{,}3 \cdot 10^5\) (\(1{,}7 \cdot 10^{17}\) against \(5 \cdot 10^{11}\)). If we assume that one operation takes \(10^{-9}\) s (an assumption, not a measurement, but it agrees with the table in KREYSZIG, PDF p. 877, where for \(\tfrac23 n^3\) operations the time is \(0{,}7\) s at \(n = 1000\) and \(11\) min at \(n = 10\,000\)), the first computation takes about \(170\) s and the second \(0{,}05\) s. Figure 7.32 shows all this on one graph.

The band also saves memory. Since the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is symmetric, it is enough to store the diagonal and the entries below it or above it (ONATE1, appendix B, paragraph after equation (B.9), PDF p. 448: "It is sufficient to store only the coefficients above (or below) the principal diagonal and the diagonal coefficients"), which nearly halves the memory and the work. Profile storage (profile) by COOK, PDF p. 57 saves still more: for every row we store the entries from the first nonzero one to the diagonal, also the zeros in between, because the elimination fills them ("Zeros between the skyline and the diagonal are retained because a direct (noniterative) equation solver creates fills"). For the bridge, below the diagonal and with it there are \(231\) entries, in the band \(140\) in the numbering along the span and \(210\) in the numbering by rows, and in the profile \(88\) and \(140\). The triangle \(\mat L\) has \(83\) and \(121\) entries (above) and all of them lie in the profile, which tells us that the fill does not escape the profile (checked on this example, we do not prove the general statement).

7.8.3 Renumbering the unknowns (preštevilčenje neznank)

The numbering of the unknowns is our choice, but the band, the fill and the cost depend on it. May we renumber the unknowns arbitrarily without changing the solution? Let us look at the smallest case first. For the truss of two bars from section 7.5.2, which meet at the point \(C\), with the unknowns of this point in the order \(x\), then \(y\), we have \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{smallmatrix}\right] \cdot 10^6\) N/m. If we swap them, the matrix becomes \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1{,}4112 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 7{,}4088 \end{smallmatrix}\right] \cdot 10^6\) N/m, and the right-hand side and the solution are swapped. We will do the same with a matrix of any order, so we write the notion in general.

Definition 7.45 Permutation matrix (permutacijska matrika)

Let \(\pi\) be a rearrangement of the numbers \(1, \dots, n\), that is a sequence \(\pi(1), \dots, \pi(n)\) in which every number from \(1\) to \(n\) appears exactly once. The permutation matrix (permutacijska matrika) \(\mat P\) of order \(n\) of the rearrangement \(\pi\) is the matrix with entries

\[P_{\mathrm{ij}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } j = \pi(i) , \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} . \end{cases}\]

In every row and every column there is therefore exactly one one, the rest are zeros. For a column \(\vek d\), \((\mat P\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} = d_{\pi(\mathrm{i})}\): in the column \(\mat P\,\vek d\) the unknown with the new number \(i\) has the old number \(\pi(i)\).

Source: The definition is ours. The notion in this form is not from the sources of the book. COOK, PDF p. 57 mentions that programs renumber the unknowns themselves ("renumbering option") and convert the results back to the input numbering.

Lemma 7.46 Renumbering does not change the solution (preštevilčenje ne spremeni rešitve)

Let \(\mat P\) be the permutation matrix of a rearrangement \(\pi\) of order \(n\), \(\mat K\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\) and \(\vek f\) a column. Then:

  1. \(\mat P\,\mat P^\T = \mat I\) (the identity matrix, definition 1.105).
  2. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat K} = \mat P\,\mat K\,\mat P^\T\) has entries \(\tilde K_{\mathrm{ij}} = K_{\pi(\mathrm{i})\,\pi(\mathrm{j})}\), is symmetric and positive definite.
  3. If \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\), then \(\tilde{\mat K}\,(\mat P\,\vek d) = \mat P\,\vek f\). The system \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\tilde{\vek d} = \mat P\,\vek f\) has exactly one solution \(\tilde{\vek d} = \mat P\,\vek d\).
Proof

We must show the three points of the lemma, each by the definition of the permutation matrix and the rules for the product and the transpose (lemmas 1.99 and 1.101).

  1. The entry \((\mat P\,\mat P^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} P_{\mathrm{ik}}\,P_{\mathrm{jk}}\). The term \(k\) is nonzero only for \(k = \pi(i)\) and at the same time \(k = \pi(j)\). Since in a rearrangement every number occurs only once, this holds only for \(i = j\), and then the sum is \(1\). So \(\mat P\,\mat P^\T = \mat I\). Likewise \((\mat P^\T\mat P)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} P_{\mathrm{ki}}\,P_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is nonzero only for \(i = \pi(k) = j\), and for every \(i\) there is exactly one such \(k\), so also \(\mat P^\T\mat P = \mat I\).
  2. The entry \((\mat P\,\mat K\,\mat P^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{l}} P_{\mathrm{ik}}\,K_{\mathrm{kl}}\,P_{\mathrm{jl}}\) is nonzero only for \(k = \pi(i)\) and \(l = \pi(j)\), and equals \(K_{\pi(\mathrm{i})\,\pi(\mathrm{j})}\). Since \(\mat K\) is symmetric, \(K_{\pi(\mathrm{j})\,\pi(\mathrm{i})} = K_{\pi(\mathrm{i})\,\pi(\mathrm{j})}\), so \(\tilde{\mat K}\) is symmetric.
  3. Let \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) and \(\vek y = \mat P^\T\vek x\). By point 1, \(\mat P\,\vek y = \mat P\,\mat P^\T\vek x = \vek x \ne \vek 0\), so \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\). By the rule for the transposed product, \(\vek x^\T\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek x = (\mat P^\T\vek x)^\T\mat K\,(\mat P^\T\vek x) = \vek y^\T\mat K\,\vek y > 0\), because \(\mat K\) is positive definite. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat K}\) is positive definite.
  4. If \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\), we multiply from the left by \(\mat P\) and insert \(\mat I = \mat P^\T\mat P\) (point 1) in front of \(\vek d\): \(\mat P\,\mat K\,\mat P^\T\mat P\,\vek d = \mat P\,\vek f\). This is \(\tilde{\mat K}\,(\mat P\,\vek d) = \mat P\,\vek f\).
  5. By point 3 and theorem 6.29 the system \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\tilde{\vek d} = \mat P\,\vek f\) has exactly one solution. By point 4, \(\mat P\,\vek d\) is a solution, so it is this one.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

For the truss of two bars, \(\mat P = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) (\(\pi = (2, 1)\)), and the matrix \(\tilde{\mat K}\) has the pivots \(1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\) and \(7{,}4088 - 1{,}8816^2/1{,}4112 = 4{,}9\) (\(\cdot 10^6\) N/m), and with the original numbering \(7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\) and \(0{,}9333 \cdot 10^6\) N/m. The pivots are different, but their product is \(6{,}9149\) in both cases (for a matrix of order \(2\) it is \(ad - b^2\), which does not change under the swap), and the solution is the same, only in another order. For the bridge \(\mat P\) has order \(21\) with the rearrangement \(\pi = (1, 2, 12, 13, 3, 4, 14, 15, 5, 6, 16, 17, \dots)\) (the number in the numbering along the span, the corresponding number in the numbering by rows): the unknown \(u\) of node \(t_1\) is third along the span and twelfth by rows. The computation confirms \(\mat P\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\text{(rows)}}\,\mat P^\T = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\text{(span)}}\) with exactly equal entries and \(\mat P\,\vek d^{\text{(rows)}} = \vek d^{\text{(span)}}\), with the largest displacement \(7{,}305\) mm (the displacement \(v\) of node \(b_3\) from section 7.7). Renumbering changes only the band, the fill and the cost (\(7\) against \(14\), \(26\) against \(64\), \(210\) against \(480\) operations), but not the solution. Programs renumber the unknowns themselves (COOK, PDF p. 57, "renumbering option"), and the book does not treat the procedures for it.

For what follows we need one more form of the same elimination. For a structure we often have to solve several load cases with the same matrix, for the bridge for example a load on half of the span or wind. Must we eliminate anew every time? No, if we remember the multipliers and pivots of the elimination.

Lemma 7.47 Triangular and diagonal factorization (razcep na trikotni in diagonalni faktor)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\). Let \(\mat L\) be the lower triangular matrix with ones on the diagonal in which column \(k\) below the diagonal is the column of multipliers \(\vek g/K_{11}\) of the \(k\)-th step of elimination, and \(\mat D\) the diagonal matrix of the pivots of the \(k\)-th steps from theorem 6.29. Then

\[\mat K = \mat L\,\mat D\,\mat L^\T . \tag{7.45}\]
Proof

We prove it by induction on the order \(n\) (theorem 1.44). The statement \(P(n)\): for every symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\) the equality (7.45) holds.

  1. Start, \(n = 1\): \(\mat K = [K_{11}]\), \(\mat L = [1]\), \(\mat D = [K_{11}]\).
  2. Induction step. Let \(P(n - 1)\) hold. We write \(\mat K = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} K_{11} & \vek g^\T \\ \vek g & \mat K' \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and \(\vek\ell = \vek g/K_{11}\). The matrix \(\mat K'' = \mat K' - \vek g\,\vek g^\T/K_{11}\) is symmetric positive definite of order \(n - 1\) (theorem 6.29, steps 5 and 6). By \(P(n - 1)\), \(\mat K'' = \mat L''\mat D''\mat L''^\T\) for the factorization determined by the multipliers and pivots of \(\mat K''\).
  3. The first step of elimination of the matrix \(\mat K\) gives the multipliers \(\vek\ell\) and the pivot \(K_{11}\), and the further steps are the steps of elimination of the matrix \(\mat K''\) (step 4 of the proof of theorem 6.29). Therefore \(\mat L = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & \vek 0^\T \\ \vek\ell & \mat L'' \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and \(\mat D = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} K_{11} & \vek 0^\T \\ \vek 0 & \mat D'' \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), where \(\mat L''\) and \(\mat D''\) are the multipliers and pivots of the matrix \(\mat K''\).
  4. Block multiplication gives \(\mat L\,\mat D = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} K_{11} & \vek 0^\T \\ K_{11}\vek\ell & \mat L''\mat D'' \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and
    \[\mat L\,\mat D\,\mat L^\T = \begin{bmatrix} K_{11} & K_{11}\,\vek\ell^\T \\ K_{11}\,\vek\ell & K_{11}\,\vek\ell\,\vek\ell^\T + \mat L''\mat D''\mat L''^\T \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} K_{11} & \vek g^\T \\ \vek g & \vek g\,\vek g^\T/K_{11} + \mat K'' \end{bmatrix} = \mat K ,\]
    because \(K_{11}\vek\ell = \vek g\), \(K_{11}\vek\ell\,\vek\ell^\T = \vek g\,\vek g^\T/K_{11}\) and \(\vek g\,\vek g^\T/K_{11} + \mat K'' = \mat K'\).
  5. By the principle of induction \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n\).

Source: The factorization is named by KREYSZIG §20.2, PDF p. 878 to 881, and ONATE1, appendix B, equations (B.2), (B.3) and (B.7), (B.8), PDF p. 446 to 447 ("forward elimination", "back substitution"). The source has the factorization \(\mat L\mat U\), KREYSZIG on PDF p. 881 for a symmetric positive definite matrix the Cholesky form \(\mat A = \mat L\mat L^\T\). The proof in steps is not from the sources.

By lemma 7.42 the matrix \(\mat L\) has the same band as \(\mat K\) (the column \(\vek\ell\) has at most \(b\) nonzero entries), and the numbers \(83\) and \(121\) of nonzero entries in figure 7.31 are the entries of the matrix \(\mat L\) below the diagonal together with it. We solve the system \(\mat K\,\vek x = \vek f\) in three steps: \(\mat L\,\vek y = \vek f\) from top to bottom (forward, forward elimination), \(\mat D\,\vek z = \vek y\) with divisions, and \(\mat L^\T\vek x = \vek z\) from bottom to top (backward, back substitution). In row \(i\) the first step takes \(i - 1\) multiplications, \(n(n - 1)/2\) in all, the same for the third (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 877: for the unknown \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) there are \(n - i\) multiplications), so about \(n^2\) for a full matrix and \(2 n b\) for a banded one. For \(n = 10^4\) and \(b = 100\) this is \(10^8\) multiplications for a full and \(2 \cdot 10^6\) for a banded matrix, while the factorization cost \(1{,}7 \cdot 10^{11}\) and \(5 \cdot 10^7\) respectively. We do the factorization once, and every further load case costs only this much (ONATE1, PDF p. 448: "several solutions for different right-hand sides \(f\) can be obtained ... This process is often called a resolution since it is not necessary to recompute the \(L\) and \(U\) arrays").

For the truss of two bars with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) from section 7.5.2, \(\ell_{21} = -1{,}8816/7{,}4088 = -0{,}2540\) and \(\mat D = \mathrm{diag}(7{,}4088,\ 0{,}9333) \cdot 10^6\) N/m. For the load \(10\) kN downward at the point \(C\), \(\vek f = (0, -10\,000)\) N, \(\vek y = (0, -10\,000)\) N, \(\vek z = (0, -10{,}714)\) mm, \(\vek x = (-2{,}721,\ -10{,}714)\) mm, as in section 7.5.2. For the second case, \(10\) kN horizontally in the direction \(+x\), we use the same \(\mat L\) and \(\mat D\): \(\vek y = (10\,000,\ 2540)\) N, \(\vek z = (1{,}350,\ 2{,}721)\) mm, \(\vek x = (2{,}041,\ 2{,}721)\) mm. The second entry of the column \(\vek x\), the displacement \(2{,}721\) mm in the direction \(y\) due to the horizontal force, is equal in magnitude to the displacement \(-2{,}721\) mm in the direction \(x\) due to an equally large vertical force (the sign differs because the vertical force points downward). So the reciprocal theorem 4.140 predicts: the displacement in the direction \(x\) due to a force in the direction \(y\) is equal to the displacement in the direction \(y\) due to a force in the direction \(x\) (the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}^{-1}\) says the same). With the same factored matrix we have thus solved both load cases, the second without a new elimination.

The solution that the computer gives is not exactly accurate. ONATE1, §3.13.4, PDF p. 137 lists three kinds of errors in the solution of the global system by a direct method. The first is ill-conditioning of the system (slaba pogojenost): small changes in \(\mat K\) or \(\vek f\) cause large changes of the solution. The second is truncation (okrajšanje): the computer stores only the first \(d\) digits of every number and so loses part of the data. The third is round-off (zaokrožitev): during the computation the computer adjusts the last digit of every number. By the source truncation is more important than round-off. In chapter 6 we measured the conditioning by the condition number \(\kappa(\mat K)\) (definition 6.31): the relative error of the solution can be up to \(\kappa\) times larger than the relative error of the right-hand side. For the truss of two bars the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) are \(0{,}870 \cdot 10^6\) and \(7{,}950 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, so \(\kappa = 9{,}14\): we lose less than one digit of about sixteen. For the bridge \(\kappa = 395\), equal in both numberings, because the eigenvalues do not change under renumbering: if \(\mat K\,\vek v = \lambda\,\vek v\), then \(\mat P\,\mat K\,\mat P^\T(\mat P\,\vek v) = \mat P\,\mat K\,\vek v = \lambda\,\mat P\,\vek v\). The hat functions of the bar from chapter 6 gave \(\kappa = 29\), \(113\) and \(438\) for \(4\), \(8\) and \(16\) elements and \(\kappa \approx 1{,}7\,n^2\). If the pattern continues, for \(10^4\) elements \(\kappa\) would be about \(1{,}7 \cdot 10^8\) and we would lose about eight of sixteen digits. The source (ONATE1, PDF p. 137) names as the main cause of ill-conditioning an element of large stiffness connected to elements of much smaller stiffness. The smallest example is two bars in a row, the first with stiffness \(k_1\) fixed to the wall, the second with \(k_2\) at the end of the first. The matrix of free unknowns is \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} k_1 + k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\), and for \(k_1/k_2 = 10^6\) we have \(\kappa \approx 10^6\), for \(k_1/k_2 = 10^3\) we have \(\kappa \approx 10^3\). A stiffness ratio of \(10^6\) between neighbouring elements thus costs six digits of sixteen.

7.9 Temperature and bars of wrong length

The steel bar that we heated by 30 K in section 3.3.3 was pressed by two rigid walls with a force of 6927 N, because the walls did not let it lengthen. A bar in a truss is not clamped between rigid walls. Its ends are nodes, which move if the rest of the truss lets them. What does heating do to a truss? And what if a bar was made a millimetre too long and we must fit it into a place that is a millimetre shorter? In both cases no external force acts on the truss, yet the nodes move and forces can appear in the bars. We do not need a new theorem for this. Only the relation between the strain and the force in a bar must change, and everything else, the matrix \(\mat K\), assembly, supports and reactions, stays as in sections 7.1 to 7.5.

The model is the same as before. The truss is made of steel bars with pins (definition 4.4), \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K, and the axial stiffness \(EA\) is constant in each bar. The temperature of each bar is constant along the bar and differs by \(\Delta T\) from the reference temperature, at which the truss is free of stress, so the bar has the thermal strain of definition 3.13. Displacements are small, and everything is computed on the shape before loading (section 7.5). The examples from chapters 4 and 5 are already known: the wall truss with bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) (loaded with \(10\) kN, \(A = 1\ \text{cm}^2\) in each bar, \(EA = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N) and the same truss with the post \(CD\) (section 4.7.5).

7.9.1 Initial strain (začetna deformacija)

Take a single bar with no forces at its ends. If we heat it, it lengthens by \(\alpha\,\Delta T\,L\) and there is no force. If it was made \(\delta\) too long, its length without force is \(L + \delta\), and if we place it into a gap of length \(L\), it would have, measured against the gap, the strain \(\delta/L\) without a force. What the two bars have in common is that they would have a strain different from zero even if nothing acted on them. The relation between force and strain of a bar must therefore measure the strain from this value onward.

Definition 7.48 Initial strain (začetna deformacija)

Let a bar with axial stiffness \(EA\) be fitted between two nodes at distance \(L\), and let \(\varepsilon\) be its strain, that is the elongation between the nodes divided by \(L\) (a number without a unit). The initial strain (začetna deformacija) of the bar is the number \(\varepsilon_0\) at which the axial force of the bar is zero when \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\), and the axial force is

\[N = EA\,(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_0) . \tag{7.46}\]

For a bar heated by \(\Delta T\) relative to the reference temperature, \(\varepsilon_0 = \alpha\,\Delta T\). For a bar that is \(\delta\) longer than the distance \(L\) between the nodes it connects, \(\varepsilon_0 = \delta/L\).

Source: FELIPPA (4.16) to (4.18) (PDF p. 58), COOK §2.10, (2.10-1) (PDF p. 67), ONATE1 (4.17) (PDF p. 147). A bar that is too long is not in the sources, we get it from the same relation.

Relation (7.46) is the one-dimensional row of Hooke's law with temperature (theorem 3.15). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) we have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E + \alpha\,\Delta T\), hence \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \alpha\,\Delta T)\), and the axial force is the stress times the cross-section, \(N = A\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). It means only that in every step where we previously wrote \(N = EA\,\varepsilon\) we subtract \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\). For the bar between walls from section 3.3.3 we have \(\varepsilon = 0\), so \(N = -EA\,\varepsilon_0 = -EA\,\alpha\,\Delta T\), which is equation (3.18) multiplied by the cross-section. If the temperature varies along the bar, we take the average temperature of the bar. COOK shows that a linear temperature distribution, inserted as an initial stress at the ends, gives a stress that varies along the element, although it must be constant in the element, and therefore recommends the average temperature (COOK, PDF pp. 67-68).

The numbers we will need: for the steel bar from chapter 3 (\(EA = 1{,}5394 \cdot 10^7\) N, \(\Delta T = 30\) K) we have \(\varepsilon_0 = 15 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 30 = 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(EA\,\varepsilon_0 = 6927\) N. For a bar of the wall truss (\(EA = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N) at the same temperature change \(EA\,\varepsilon_0 = 8820\) N. For the post \(CD\) of length \(3\) m that is \(1\) mm too long, \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\ \text{mm}/3\ \text{m} = 3{,}33 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(EA\,\varepsilon_0 = 6533\) N.

7.9.2 Nodal forces of an initial strain (vozliščne sile začetne deformacije)

How does the initial strain enter the equations of the method? Imagine an element whose nodes are prevented from moving in any way. A heated element would like to lengthen, but the nodes do not let it, so it is compressed with the force \(-EA\,\varepsilon_0\), like the bar between walls. The nodes must therefore hold it with forces that compress it. By the law of action and reaction the element pushes the nodes outwards with the same force \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\). When the nodes are not fixed, these forces act on them as a load. The following lemma states this exactly. It holds for a bar on the axis \(x\) and for a bar of a truss, where \(\vek n\) is the unit vector from the first node of the bar to the second (section 7.5.1).

Lemma 7.49 Nodal forces of an initial strain (vozliščne sile začetne deformacije)

Let element \(e\) be a straight bar of length \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\) with linear shape functions (definition 7.2), constant axial stiffness \(EA\) and constant initial strain \(\varepsilon_0\) (definition 7.48). Let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the column of displacements of its nodes, for a truss in global axes, and \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}} = \begin{bmatrix}\vek n^\T & \vek 0^\T \\ \vek 0^\T & \vek n^\T\end{bmatrix}\) the matrix from lemma 7.28, which gives the axial displacements of the nodes from the global ones, \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (for a bar on the axis \(x\), \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the identity matrix and \(\vek n = 1\)). Then:

  1. The virtual displacement equation of the bar has, because of \(\varepsilon_0\), an additional term \(\int EA\,\varepsilon_0\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) on the right-hand side.
  2. The element contributes to the right-hand side the nodal forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-1, 1)^\T\) in the axis of the bar and \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-\vek n, \vek n)^\T\) in global axes.
  3. The equations of the structure are \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek f_0\), where \(\vek f_0 = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0}\) (theorem 7.13).
  4. The axial force of the element is \(N_{\mathrm{e}} = EA\,\big(\vek n\cdot(\vek u_2 - \vek u_1)/L_{\mathrm{e}} - \varepsilon_0\big)\), where \(\vek u_1\) and \(\vek u_2\) are the displacements of its nodes.
Proof

We must show that the initial strain changes only the right-hand side of the equations and the force of the element, not the matrix.

  1. By definition 7.48 the axial force of the bar is \(N = EA\,(u' - \varepsilon_0)\), because the strain of the bar is \(u'\).
  2. Theorem 4.76 requires only \(N' + q = 0\) and \(N(L) = F\) and does not use the relation between \(N\) and \(u\) (steps 2 to 5 of its proof). Hence for every virtual displacement \(w\) we have \(\int N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L)\). Where \(EA\) and \(\varepsilon_0\) are constant only piecewise, we apply the theorem on each piece separately and add the pieces, as for the weak form (definition 6.2).
  3. We insert \(N\) from step 1 and move the term with \(\varepsilon_0\) to the right:
    \[\int EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L) + \int EA\,\varepsilon_0\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{7.47}\]
    This is claim 1. The left side is the same as in equation (6.2), so the matrix of the element is the same. The solution of the method is the solution of this equation on the trial fields (equation (6.28)).
  4. On element \(e\) of length \(h = L_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(w' = \mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}} = (-1, 1)/h\) (lemma 7.5). The additional term is therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{e}} EA\,\varepsilon_0\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,EA\,\varepsilon_0 \int_{\mathrm{e}} \mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-1, 1)^\T ,\]
    because \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\) is constant and the integral of a constant function over the length \(h\) equals its value times \(h\) (theorem 3.40). The column next to \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\) is \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0}\), as for consistent nodal forces (definition 7.7).
  5. For a truss the axial displacements are \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), the test function has the axial displacements \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\), so the additional term is \((\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}\vek w_{\mathrm{e}})^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = \vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0}\). The columns of \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\) are \((\vek n, \vek 0)\) and \((\vek 0, \vek n)\), so \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T(a, b)^\T = (a\,\vek n, b\,\vek n)\) and \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-\vek n, \vek n)\). This is claim 2.
  6. Assembly (theorem 7.13) combines the contributions of the elements on the right-hand side term by term in the same way as it combined \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\). This is claim 3.
  7. Claim 4 is step 1 with the strain \(\varepsilon = \vek n\cdot(\vek u_2 - \vek u_1)/L_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is the axial elongation \(\vek n\cdot(\vek u_2 - \vek u_1)\) divided by the length (lemma 7.28, step 1).

Source: COOK §2.10 (2.10-1) to (2.10-8) (PDF pp. 66-68), FELIPPA §4.2.2 (4.19) to (4.24) (PDF p. 59), ONATE1 §4 (PDF p. 147). The proof from theorem 4.76 is not from a source.

What have we shown? The initial strain does not change the matrix \(\mat K\), but it changes the right-hand side of the equations and the force of the element. A bar with \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\) pushes its nodes apart with \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\) in the direction of its axis (the column \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-\vek n, \vek n)\) has \(+\vek n\) at the second node). COOK proceeds in the same way: he computes the initial stresses with prevented displacements, assembles them as a load and then solves (COOK, PDF p. 66, steps 1 to 3). Mechanical forces and forces of the initial strain are added on the same right-hand side (COOK, PDF p. 66).

The trap is the term \(-EA\,\varepsilon_0\) in claim 4. For loading with forces it was not there, so it is easy to forget. If we forget it, we get a force in a bar on which nobody acts. We test this on a free bar.

7.9.3 Bar between walls and free bar (palica med stenama in prosta palica)

Take the bar from section 3.3.3, of length \(L = 10\) m, with \(EA = 1{,}5394 \cdot 10^7\) N and \(\varepsilon_0 = 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), as one element with nodes at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). The nodal forces of the initial strain are

\[\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = EA\,\varepsilon_0\,(-1, 1)^\T = (-6927, 6927)^\T\ \text{N} .\]

If both nodes are fixed (the walls), there are no free unknowns and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is an empty matrix. The reactions from section 7.3.4 are the rows of the equations \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek f_0 + \vek r\) at \(\vek d = \vek 0\) and \(\vek f = \vek 0\), so \(\vek r = -\vek f_0 = (6927, -6927)^\T\) N. The first wall pushes the bar in the direction \(+x\) and the second in the direction \(-x\), each with a force of \(6927\) N. The axial force by claim 4 is \(N = EA\,(0 - \varepsilon_0) = -6927\) N, as in chapter 3.

We remove the right wall, so that node 2 is free. The equation of node 2 is \((EA/L)\,d_2 = EA\,\varepsilon_0\), where \(EA/L = 1{,}5394 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, hence \(d_2 = \varepsilon_0\,L = 4{,}5\) mm. This is the free elongation \(\alpha\,\Delta T\,L = 15 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 30 \cdot 10\ \text{m}\) from chapter 3. The axial force by claim 4 is \(N = EA\,(d_2/L - \varepsilon_0) = 0\), as it must be. But if we forget the term \(-EA\,\varepsilon_0\), the program prints \(N = EA\,d_2/L = +6927\) N, a tensile force in a bar that lengthens freely. A test on an example where we know the solution (there is no force in a free heated bar) finds such an error. Section 7.10.2 collects such tests.

7.9.4 Statically determinate truss: displacement without forces (statično določeno paličje: premik brez sil)

In the wall truss we heat the bar \(BC\) by \(30\) K and load nothing. What happens? Node \(C\) is held by the bar \(AC\), which lies horizontally, and by the bar \(BC\). Two bars and two coordinates of the node: we can choose the lengths of both bars independently, and the node adapts. The bar \(BC\) can lengthen, and node \(C\) moves so that the bar \(AC\) stays the same length. Therefore there are no forces. We take this first as a question about all such trusses, and then test it on the wall truss.

We write the equilibrium of the free nodes with the axial forces. A bar \(e\) with the unit vector \(\vek n\) from the first node to the second has the column \(\vek h_{\mathrm{e}} = (-\vek n, \vek n)^\T\) (this is the column from lemma 7.49). A tensile force \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) pulls the first node in the direction \(+\vek n\) and the second in the direction \(-\vek n\), so with the force \(-N_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\). The column \(\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\) has components only in the displacements of the two nodes of the bar, and by assembly (theorem 7.13) we place it among all unknowns as \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\). Let \(\mat H\) be the matrix whose column \(e\) is \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\), restricted to the free unknowns (we omit the rows of the fixed unknowns), so that it has \(n_{\mathrm{f}}\) rows and \(m\) columns, and \(\vek N\) the column of the axial forces of the bars. The sum of the external force and the forces of the bars on the free nodes is zero, \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} - \sum_{\mathrm{e}} N_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek h_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), which in matrix form means

\[\mat H\,\vek N = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}} . \tag{7.48}\]

For the wall truss with the unknowns \((u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}})\) and the bars \(AC\), \(BC\) in this order, \(\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0{,}8 \\ 0 & -0{,}6 \end{bmatrix}\), because nodes \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed and only the part of the column at node \(C\), the second node of both bars, remains, that is \(+\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0)\) and \(+\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = (0{,}8, -0{,}6)\). The equation \(\mat H\,\vek N = (0, -F)^\T\) is the equation of the node from section 4.7.5 without the post. With the post, \(\mat H\) has a third column \((0, 1)^\T\).

When do the equilibrium equations alone determine the axial forces? The counting from section 7.5.3 says that this is possible only for \(m = n_{\mathrm{f}}\) (as many bars as free unknowns), but it is not sufficient, because it does not exclude a mechanism. Therefore we state static determinacy with equation (7.48) itself.

Theorem 7.50 Initial strains in a statically determinate truss (začetne deformacije v statično določenem paličju)

Let the truss have \(m\) bars and \(n_{\mathrm{f}}\) free unknowns, let \(\mat H\) be the \(n_{\mathrm{f}} \times m\) matrix from equation (7.48), let \(\mat D = \mathrm{diag}(EA_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}})\) and let \(\vek c\) be the column with entries \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = EA_{\mathrm{e}}\,\varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\). The truss is statically determinate (statično določeno) when the equation \(\mat H\,\vek N = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\) has exactly one solution \(\vek N\) for every column \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\), that is when the axial forces of the bars are determined by the equilibrium of the nodes alone, for every load. Let the truss be statically determinate, let no external force act on it, let the fixed displacements be zero and let bar \(e\) have the initial strain \(\varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.48). Then \(m = n_{\mathrm{f}}\), the matrix \(\mat H\) is invertible, the equation of the method \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_{0,\mathrm{f}}\) has exactly one solution, the axial forces of all bars are zero, and the displacements of the free nodes are such that each bar lengthens by its free elongation \(\varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Proof

We must show that under these assumptions \(\mat H\) is invertible, that the equation of the method is then solved by a displacement at which every axial force is zero, and that there is no other solution.

  1. For \(j = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{f}}\) let \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}\) be the only solution of the equation \(\mat H\,\vek b_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is column \(j\) of the identity matrix of order \(n_{\mathrm{f}}\) (by the definition of static determinacy it exists and is unique). The matrix \(\mat B\) with columns \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}\) has size \(m \times n_{\mathrm{f}}\) and \(\mat H\,\mat B = \mat I_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{f}}\), because column \(j\) of the product is \(\mat H\,\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}\) (definition 1.98).
  2. For every column \(\vek N\) of length \(m\), \(\vek N\) and \(\mat B\,\mat H\,\vek N\) are solutions of the equation \(\mat H\,\vek X = \mat H\,\vek N\), since \(\mat H\,(\mat B\,\mat H\,\vek N) = (\mat H\,\mat B)\,\mat H\,\vek N = \mat H\,\vek N\). The solution is unique, so \(\mat B\,\mat H\,\vek N = \vek N\). For \(\vek N\) equal to the columns of the identity matrix of order \(m\) we get \(\mat B\,\mat H = \mat I_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  3. We compute the sum of the diagonal entries in two ways: \(n_{\mathrm{f}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\mat H\,\mat B)_{\mathrm{ii}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,B_{\mathrm{ji}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} B_{\mathrm{ji}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat B\,\mat H)_{\mathrm{jj}} = m\). The matrix \(\mat H\) is therefore square, and by steps 1 and 2 \(\mat B\) is its inverse matrix (definition 1.107). Also \(\mat H^\T\) is invertible, because by lemma 1.101 \(\mat H^\T\mat B^\T = (\mat B\,\mat H)^\T = \mat I\) and \(\mat B^\T\mat H^\T = (\mat H\,\mat B)^\T = \mat I\). The matrix \(\mat D\) is invertible, because it is diagonal with positive entries, \(\mat D^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(L_{\mathrm{e}}/EA_{\mathrm{e}})\).
  4. By lemma 7.28 \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = (EA_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}})\,\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\). After assembly (theorem 7.13) and restriction to the free unknowns, entry \((i, k)\) of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is the sum over the bars \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} H_{\mathrm{ie}}\,D_{\mathrm{e}}\,H_{\mathrm{ke}}\), which is entry \((i, k)\) of the product \(\mat H\,\mat D\,\mat H^\T\). Hence \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat H\,\mat D\,\mat H^\T\).
  5. By lemma 7.49, claim 3, the right-hand side without external forces is \(\vek f_0 = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0}\), and since \(\mat T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0} = EA_{\mathrm{e}}\,\varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\,\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}\), its part for the free unknowns is \(\vek f_{0,\mathrm{f}} = \mat H\,\vek c\).
  6. Let \(\vek d^* = (\mat H^\T)^{-1}\mat D^{-1}\vek c\). Then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d^* = \mat H\,\mat D\,\mat H^\T(\mat H^\T)^{-1}\mat D^{-1}\vek c = \mat H\,\vek c = \vek f_{0,\mathrm{f}}\), so \(\vek d^*\) solves the equation of the method.
  7. There is no other solution. If \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek y = \vek 0\), then \(\mat H\,\mat D\,\mat H^\T\vek y = \vek 0\). Multiplying by \(\mat H^{-1}\), then by \(\mat D^{-1}\) and then by \((\mat H^\T)^{-1}\) gives \(\vek y = \vek 0\). The difference of two solutions solves this equation, so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek d^*\).
  8. By lemma 7.49, claim 4, with zero fixed displacements, \(N_{\mathrm{e}} = EA_{\mathrm{e}}\,\big(\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}} - \varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\big)\), because \(\vek h_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek n\cdot(\vek u_2 - \vek u_1)\). In a column this is \(\vek N = \mat D\,\mat H^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} - \vek c\). For \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek d^*\) we get \(\vek N = \mat D\,\mat H^\T(\mat H^\T)^{-1}\mat D^{-1}\vek c - \vek c = \vek c - \vek c = \vek 0\).
  9. From \(\mat H^\T\vek d^* = \mat D^{-1}\vek c\), for every bar \(\vek n\cdot(\vek u_2 - \vek u_1) = c_{\mathrm{e}}/D_{\mathrm{e}} = \varepsilon_{0,\mathrm{e}}\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is the free elongation of the bar.

Source: The proof is not from a source. The converse, that in a statically indeterminate truss heating causes internal forces, is stated by FELIPPA (PDF p. 56, §4.2).

What have we shown? Because \(\vek N = \mat D\,\mat H^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} - \vek c\), we have \(\mat H\,\vek N = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} - \vek f_{0,\mathrm{f}}\), so the equations of the method are the equilibrium of the nodes \(\mat H\,\vek N = \vek 0\), in which the forces of the bars are computed from the displacements. In a truss that the equilibrium alone determines, this equilibrium has only the solution \(\vek N = \vek 0\), and heating shows itself only in the displacements.

We test it on the wall truss with the heated bar \(BC\) (figure 7.33). The unit vector from \(B\) to \(C\) is \(\vek n = (0{,}8, -0{,}6)\), and \(EA\,\varepsilon_0 = 8820\) N. The nodal force of the initial strain at \(C\) is

\[EA\,\varepsilon_0\,\vek n = 8820 \cdot (0{,}8, -0{,}6) = (7056, -5292)\ \text{N} ,\]

and the opposite one at \(B\), but \(B\) is fixed. The equation \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_{0,\mathrm{f}}\) with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) from section 7.5.2 is

\[\begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix} \cdot 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}\ \begin{pmatrix} u_{\mathrm{C}} \\ v_{\mathrm{C}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 7056 \\ -5292 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{N} ,\]

and the solution is \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -3{,}75\) mm. Check in the first row: \(-1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6 \cdot (-3{,}75 \cdot 10^{-3}) = 7056\) N. The axial forces by claim 4 are

\[\begin{aligned} N_{\mathrm{AC}} &= EA\,\Big(\frac{(1, 0)\cdot(0, -3{,}75\ \text{mm})}{4\ \text{m}} - 0\Big) = 0 , \\ N_{\mathrm{BC}} &= EA\,\Big(\frac{(0{,}8, -0{,}6)\cdot(0, -3{,}75\ \text{mm})}{5\ \text{m}} - 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\Big) \\ &= EA\,(4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4} - 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}) = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The bar \(BC\) lengthened by \(2{,}25\) mm, which is \(\alpha\,\Delta T\,L = 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 5\ \text{m}\). The reactions are zero, because the axial forces are zero. Why did the node drop by exactly \(3{,}75\) mm? The bar \(AC\) stays \(4\) m long, so \(C\) moves perpendicular to it, vertically, and the vertical displacement \(v\) lengthens \(BC\) by \(0{,}6\,|v|\). The condition \(0{,}6\,|v| = 2{,}25\) mm gives \(|v| = 3{,}75\) mm.

The theorem holds in linear theory, and this has a limit. Node \(C\) in fact moves along a circular arc about \(A\) (figure 7.33), while linear theory moves it along the tangent to the arc, vertically. The bar \(AC\) therefore lengthens by \(v^2/(2 \cdot 4\ \text{m}) = 1{,}8\) µm, which is \(0{,}08\) % of the free elongation \(2{,}25\) mm. This is a term of second order in the displacement, which equation (4.48) neglects.

7.9.5 Statically indeterminate truss: forces without a load (statično nedoločeno paličje: sile brez bremena)

We add to the wall truss the post \(CD\) of length \(3\) m (section 4.7.5, figure 7.34). We take the bars in the order \(AC\), \(BC\) and \(DC\) (the post as an element with nodes \(D\) and \(C\) in this order), so that the post has the unit vector \(\vek n = (0, 1)\) from the ground to the node. The unknowns are \((u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}})\), the matrix \(\mat H\) has two rows and three columns, \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0 & -0{,}6 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and the equation \(\mat H\,\vek N = \vek 0\) has more solutions, so the truss is not statically determinate (in the sense above: \(m = 3 \ne 2 = n_{\mathrm{f}}\)). Section 4.7.5 wrote them with the unknown \(X = N_{\mathrm{CD}}\): without a load, \(\vek N = X\,(-\tfrac43, \tfrac53, 1)\). Theorem 7.50 therefore does not hold (the matrix \(\mat H\) is not square), and equilibrium does not say which \(X\) is the right one. This is told by the computation of the method, which requires that the elongations of the bars come from one displacement of the node.

We heat the post by \(30\) K, without a load. The nodal force of the initial strain at \(C\) is \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\,\vek n = (0, 8820)\) N: the heated post pushes node \(C\) upward. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is now

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 7{,}9445 \end{bmatrix} \cdot 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} ,\]

where the post contributes \(EA/L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7/3 = 6{,}5333 \cdot 10^6\) N/m to the entry \((2, 2)\), \(1{,}4112 + 6{,}5333 = 7{,}9445\). The solution is \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}300\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 1{,}181\) mm, with axial forces

\[\begin{aligned} N_{\mathrm{AC}} &= 1{,}470\ \text{kN} , \qquad N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -1{,}838\ \text{kN} , \\ N_{\mathrm{CD}} &= EA\,\Big(\frac{1{,}18125\ \text{mm}}{3\ \text{m}} - 4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\Big) = -1{,}1025\ \text{kN} . \end{aligned}\]

These are indeed solutions \(\vek N = X\,(-\tfrac43, \tfrac53, 1)\) with \(X = -1{,}1025\) kN: \(-\tfrac43 \cdot (-1{,}1025) = 1{,}470\) and \(\tfrac53 \cdot (-1{,}1025) = -1{,}8375\). The method chose one of the solutions of equilibrium, and since no external force acts, the forces of the heated post balance only each other (figure 7.34, right): the bar \(AC\) pulls node \(C\) toward \(A\) with \(1470\) N, the bar \(BC\) pushes it with a force of \(1837{,}5\) N in the direction \((0{,}8, -0{,}6)\), that is with components \((1470, -1102{,}5)\) N, and the post pushes it upward with \(1102{,}5\) N. Horizontally \(-1470 + 1470 = 0\) and vertically \(-1102{,}5 + 1102{,}5 = 0\).

If the post were between two rigid bases, it would carry \(-EA\,\alpha\,\Delta T = -8{,}82\) kN (chapter 3, equation (3.18)). But it carries only \(1{,}1025\) kN, which is \(12{,}5\) % of this force. Why? The post cannot lengthen by its free elongation \(\varepsilon_0\,L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 1{,}35\) mm, because it must move node \(C\), which is held by the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\). The node moved upward by only \(1{,}181\) mm, the post lengthened by \(1{,}181\) mm of \(1{,}35\) mm, and the remaining \(0{,}169\) mm is compressed. How stiffly does the wall truss hold the node? From the first row of the node equation we express \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = (1{,}8816/7{,}4088)\,v_{\mathrm{C}}\) and insert it in the second row:

\[\Big(7{,}9445 - \frac{1{,}8816^2}{7{,}4088}\Big) \cdot 10^6\ v_{\mathrm{C}} = 8820\ \text{N} , \qquad 7{,}4667 \cdot 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}\ v_{\mathrm{C}} = 8820\ \text{N} .\]

Of the vertical stiffness \(7{,}4667 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, \(k_{\mathrm{s}} = 6{,}5333 \cdot 10^6\) N/m belongs to the post, and to the wall truss without the post \(k_{\mathrm{p}} = 1{,}4112 - 1{,}8816^2/7{,}4088 = 0{,}9333 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, which is the second pivot of the elimination of the wall truss from section 7.5.2. The bar \(AC\) is horizontal, so the node can also adapt horizontally when it moves upward, and this adaptation is already counted in the pivot. The post and the truss are like two springs that both hold node \(C\), which moves by \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = EA\,\varepsilon_0/(k_{\mathrm{p}} + k_{\mathrm{s}})\). The force of the post is its stiffness times the difference between the displacement of the node and the free elongation:

\[\begin{aligned} N_{\mathrm{CD}} &= k_{\mathrm{s}}\,\big(v_{\mathrm{C}} - \varepsilon_0\,L_{\mathrm{CD}}\big) = k_{\mathrm{s}}\,EA\,\varepsilon_0\,\Big(\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{p}} + k_{\mathrm{s}}} - \frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{s}}}\Big) \\ &= -EA\,\varepsilon_0\,\frac{k_{\mathrm{p}}}{k_{\mathrm{p}} + k_{\mathrm{s}}} = -8820\ \text{N} \cdot \frac{0{,}9333}{7{,}4667} = -1102{,}5\ \text{N} . \end{aligned}\]

The share \(k_{\mathrm{p}}/(k_{\mathrm{p}} + k_{\mathrm{s}}) = 0{,}125\) is the ratio of the stiffness of the truss to all the stiffness at the node. If the truss were infinitely stiff, the share would be \(1\) and the post would carry the whole force of the bar between walls. Because the truss is soft, the node gives way, and the post keeps an eighth.

The same computation holds if the post is \(\delta = 1\) mm too long and we fit it in. The initial strain is \(\varepsilon_0 = \delta/L_{\mathrm{CD}} = 3{,}33 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the nodal force of the initial strain at \(C\) is \(EA\,\varepsilon_0\,\vek n = (0, 6533)\) N, the displacements of the node are \(0{,}222\) mm and \(0{,}875\) mm and the forces are

\[\begin{aligned} N_{\mathrm{AC}} &= 1{,}089\ \text{kN} , \qquad N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -1{,}361\ \text{kN} , \\ N_{\mathrm{CD}} &= -6533\ \text{N} \cdot 0{,}125 = -0{,}817\ \text{kN} . \end{aligned}\]

The forces are in the ratio \(3{,}33/4{,}5 = 0{,}741\) to the heated post, because the equations are linear in \(\varepsilon_0\) (figure 7.35).

A load and a wrong length add up. The equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek f_0\) is linear in \(\vek f\) and \(\vek f_0\) and has exactly one solution, because \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite (theorem 7.33, theorem 6.29), so the solution for both loads is the sum of the solutions. For the load of \(10\) kN at \(C\) the forces are \(-1{,}667\), \(2{,}083\) and \(-8{,}750\) kN (section 4.7.5), and together with the post that is too long we get

\[\begin{aligned} N_{\mathrm{AC}} &= -1{,}667 + 1{,}089 = -0{,}578\ \text{kN} , \quad N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 2{,}083 - 1{,}361 = 0{,}722\ \text{kN} , \\ N_{\mathrm{CD}} &= -8{,}750 - 0{,}817 = -9{,}567\ \text{kN} , \end{aligned}\]

which agrees with the direct computation with both loads at once. The post is now compressed with \(9{,}567\) kN, that is with the stress \(95{,}7\) MPa, which is below the yield limit \(220\) MPa (buckling of the compressed post, as in chapter 4, we do not check). A millimetre of error in length loaded the post by \(9{,}3\) % more than the load alone.

What have we learned? Temperature and a wrong length enter the method as a right-hand side of the equations and as a term in the force of a bar. The matrix, assembly, supports and reactions are the same. In a statically determinate truss (theorem 7.50) the two effects are a displacement without forces, and in a statically indeterminate truss they are forces that the softer part takes up. Whether the computed forces are correct we check with the checks that the next section collects.

7.10 Steps of an analysis and checking the model (koraki analize in preverjanje modela)

We have done every step of the method at least once: element, assembly, supports, solution, reactions, forces in bars, temperature. Now we put them together. In what order does a program carry them out, and how do we find out that the printed solution is the right one, not merely that the program computed it? The answer to the second question is not a single test. Each test finds some errors and overlooks others, and so it is worth knowing which.

7.10.1 Steps (koraki)

The sources divide an analysis into five (ONATE1 §2.9, PDF pp. 98-99) or four steps (ONATE1 §1.5.3, PDF p. 43). FELIPPA calls the first three disconnection, localization and computation of the member equations (PDF p. 33), and COOK adds temperature (§2.10, PDF p. 66). We divide the steps a little more finely, so that every section of this chapter is in one of them. At each step we write what goes into it and what comes out.

  1. Model and idealizations (section 7.7): which assumptions we make (pins, loads at nodes, bar weight neglected) and what we draw. The result is a drawing and a list of assumptions.
  2. Nodes, elements, connectivity table (sections 7.2 and 7.5): the coordinates of the nodes (\(n_{\mathrm{v}}\) nodes in the plane, \(2\,n_{\mathrm{v}}\) numbers) and for each element the numbers of its nodes.
  3. Material and section data: \(E\), \(A\) for each element, if needed \(\alpha\) and \(\Delta T\) (section 7.9).
  4. Element matrices and loads: \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (sections 7.1, 7.4, 7.5), \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\) (section 7.1.3) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}0}\) (section 7.9). A loop over the elements.
  5. Assembly (section 7.2): \(\mat K\) and \(\vek f\) by adding according to the connectivity table, without the extended element matrices. Steps 4 and 5 are usually done together, element by element.
  6. Supports (section 7.3): separation of free and prescribed unknowns.
  7. Solution \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{fp}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{p}}\) (sections 7.3 and 7.8, chapter 6).
  8. Reactions \(\vek r\) (section 7.3.4), forces in elements \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) and stresses \(N_{\mathrm{e}}/A\) (sections 7.1.4 and 7.5).
  9. Checks (the next section).

The sequence is the same as in the program for bars shown by ONATE1: reading the data (INPUT), the element matrix (STIFFNESS), the loads (LOAD), assembly and solution (SOLVE), stresses (STRESS) (ONATE1 §3.6, fig. 3.5, PDF pp. 119-120). Figure 7.36 shows the steps and the sections in which we treated them.

For the input data of steps 2, 3 and 6 we take the bridge from section 7.7. Nodes: the bottom ones \(b_{\mathrm{i}} = (3i,\ 0)\) m for \(i = 0, \dots, 6\) and the top ones \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = (3i,\ 3)\) m for \(i = 1, \dots, 5\), in all \(12\) nodes and \(24\) unknowns. The bars (all \(A = 10\ \text{cm}^2\), \(E = 196\) GPa), \(21\) in all:

group bars number length
bottom chord \(b_{\mathrm{i}-1}b_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(i = 1, \dots, 6\) 6 \(3\) m
top chord \(t_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}+1}\), \(i = 1, \dots, 4\) 4 \(3\) m
posts \(b_{\mathrm{i}}t_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(i = 1, \dots, 5\) 5 \(3\) m
end bars \(b_0t_1\), \(b_6t_5\) 2 \(4{,}243\) m
diagonals \(t_1b_2\), \(t_2b_3\), \(t_4b_3\), \(t_5b_4\) 4 \(4{,}243\) m

Supports: \(b_0\) fixed (\(u_{\mathrm{x}} = u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\)), \(b_6\) movable (\(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\)), so \(3\) prescribed and \(21\) free unknowns. Loads: \(10\) kN downward at \(b_1, \dots, b_5\). The table is the whole input file. The computation does what is written in it, so an error in it shows itself only in the checks below.

7.10.2 Checks (preverjanja)

Checks are computations that we carry out on the result and that have a known outcome if the computation is correct. We try each by introducing one error into a correct model and looking at whether the check reports it. All the errors of this section were introduced by computer (NumPy) into models that we already know, and the numbers given are from these computations. There are eight checks.

(a) Reactions balance the loads (lemma 7.20). We add the reactions and the loads in each direction (and the moments). The sum must be zero. The check finds forgotten coupling terms: if in assembly without the links between the nodes of an element we add only the diagonal blocks of \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of the wall truss stays the same, because \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed, and the displacements \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -10{,}714\) mm are correct, but all four reactions are zero and the sum of the vertical forces is \(-10\,000\) N instead of zero. It also finds a changed sign of the off-diagonal entry in \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) (the error from check (c)): the reactions computed from the rows of the matrix \(\mat K\) with this wrong displacement have the sums \(-40\,320\) N horizontally and \(10\,240\) N vertically instead of zero. But it overlooks errors that equilibrium does not feel: if we enter \(20\) kN instead of \(10\) kN in \(b_2\) of the bridge, the reactions are \(31\,667\) N and \(28\,333\) N, their sum is \(60\,000\) N, which is the sum of the entered loads. It also overlooks a wrong half model of the bridge with a fixed support at \(b_0\) (section 7.7.3), which satisfies equilibrium (\(30 + 15 - 45 = 0\) kN horizontally and \(25 - 25 = 0\) vertically) and gives \(-5\) kN in the bottom chord instead of \(25\) kN.

(b) Symmetry. For a symmetric structure and a symmetric load the result must be symmetric (COOK, §2.11, PDF p. 69). The check finds a wrong load and a wrong coordinate. The bridge with \(20\) kN in \(b_2\) has the deflection \(-8{,}091\) mm at \(b_2\) and \(-7{,}565\) mm at \(b_4\), and the correct model \(-6{,}324\) mm at both. The space wall truss from section 7.6 has under a vertical load \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and equal forces \(-7{,}120\) kN in both oblique bars. If we enter the coordinate \(z = -1{,}4\) m instead of \(-1{,}5\) m for the second node, \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}102\) mm, the forces are \(-6{,}874\) and \(-7{,}307\) kN, and the reactions still balance (sums \(0\), \(10\,000\), \(0\) N). The check overlooks errors that are themselves symmetric: a wrong \(E\) or \(A\) in all bars and symmetric errors of the model.

(c) Energy. The work of the loads is the strain energy (theorem 4.86): \(\tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\vek f = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} N_{\mathrm{e}}^2 L_{\mathrm{e}}/(2EA)\). For the correct solution the left side equals \(\tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d\), because \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\) and \(\vek d^\T\vek r = 0\) (the reactions are nonzero only at prescribed unknowns, where \(\vek d\) is zero). By theorem 7.13 this is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), and the right side is the same sum by theorem 4.3.
