Wall truss: \(53{,}571\) J both ways, bridge \(138{,}90\) J both ways. The check finds a solution that does not solve the right system. If in \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of the wall truss we change the sign of the off-diagonal entry, \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 2{,}721\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -10{,}714\) mm, the work of the load is still \(53{,}571\) J, but the sum over the bars, computed from the true data of the elements, is \(163{,}29\) J. It overlooks errors where the solution is correct for a wrong system: the forgotten coupling terms from (a) give \(53{,}571\) J on both sides. It also overlooks wrong units and model errors, because the equality holds in every system of units and in every model: for the wall truss with mixed units from (g), \(\tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\vek f\) equals the sum over the bars. The check holds for loads without initial strains. For the heated post without a load, the work of the nodal forces of the initial strain is \(\tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\vek f_0 = 5{,}21\) J and the sum over the bars is \(0{,}744\) J, so the equality does not hold.

(d) Hand calculation (račun na roko). COOK writes: "Hand calculation is used to obtain approximate results as a check on FEA results" (PDF p. 72). We solve the wall truss with the equilibrium of node \(C\): \(-0{,}6\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -10\) kN gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}667\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}333\) kN. We solve the bridge with a section (section 7.7): the bottom chord \(b_2b_3\) carries \((25 \cdot 6 - 10 \cdot 3)/3 = 40\) kN. The hand calculation finds four of our errors: the changed sign in \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) gives \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = +13{,}333\) kN (correct \(-13{,}333\) kN), a wrong load in the bridge gives \(53{,}3\) kN in the bar \(b_2b_3\) instead of \(40\) kN, a wrong half model gives \(-5\) kN instead of \(25\) kN, mixed units give a displacement \(-2{,}7 \cdot 10^{-6}\) mm instead of \(-2{,}721\) mm (check (g)). It does not find errors of the model that the hand calculation shares with the program, such as the same pin model or the same neglected bar weight.

(e) Zero or tiny pivot. In elimination, a missing support or a mechanism produces a pivot zero (theorem 7.33, section 7.5.3). For the wall truss where we move \(B\) onto the line \(AC\) (section 7.5.3), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mathrm{diag}(9{,}8,\ 0) \cdot 10^6\) N/m and the second pivot is zero. For the bridge without the movable support at \(b_6\) the last pivot in the computer is \(-1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-9}\) N/m, and the largest \(1{,}3 \cdot 10^8\) N/m: a rounding error of zero, their ratio is \(10^{-17}\). The program must stop the computation here. COOK warns of the same phenomenon for several collinear elements on one bar: each junction is a hinge, a mechanism arises, and the program reports "small pivot" or "divide by zero" (COOK, PDF p. 72). The check finds only singularity. Data errors for which \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) stays positive definite escape it.

(f) Mesh refinement. For a bar with a load along its length the solution is not exact on any mesh (section 7.4.3). The force in the element at the clamp for the test load of that section (the load grows linearly, \(60{,}10\) N in all, it is not the self weight) is for \(1, 2, 4, 8, 16\) linear elements \(40{,}06\), \(55{,}09\), \(58{,}85\), \(59{,}78\) and \(60{,}02\) N, the exact value is \(60{,}10\) N. The changes are \(15{,}02\), \(3{,}76\), \(0{,}94\) and \(0{,}24\) N, each four times smaller than the previous one, which shows that the solution is approaching. For a truss refinement makes no sense: one bar has exact displacements by corollary 7.31, and more elements on one bar give a mechanism (COOK, PDF p. 72, and check (e)). The reaction stays \(-60{,}097\) N on every mesh, so check (a) does not detect a coarse mesh. Refinement does not find errors that do not change with the mesh, such as a wrong load and a wrong \(E\).

(g) Units. We write all quantities with units and use one system, for example N and m. For the wall truss with \(E\) in Pa (\(196 \cdot 10^9\)) and lengths in mm and the cross-section in mm\(^2\) we get the displacement \(-2{,}7 \cdot 10^{-6}\) mm instead of \(-2{,}721\) mm, while the axial forces are right (\(-13{,}333\) and \(16{,}667\) kN), because in a statically determinate truss they are determined by equilibrium. Reactions, symmetry and energy do not find such an error, a hand computation of the displacement does (section 7.5.2). FELIPPA gives the numbers of the truss example (fig. 2.4 and (3.25), PDF pp. 30, 46) without units (\(EA = 100\), \(L = 10\), displacements \(0{,}4\) and \(-0{,}2\)), so with this example we cannot check units.

(h) Element force at a support against the reaction. For the hanging bar of two elements and self weight (section 7.3.4) the reaction is \(-60{,}097\) N, which by lemma 7.20 is the whole weight \(q\,L\), and the force in the element at the clamp is \(45{,}07\) N. They do not agree because the force of an element is the average of the true \(N = q\,(L - x)\) over the element, not its value at the clamp, where it is \(60{,}10\) N. We must trust the reaction. The difference is not an error, but tells us that the mesh is coarse (check (f)).

The list collects which check found which error and which overlooked it, for the cases that we computed. Errors that we did not try with a check are marked "not tried". The checks are named as above: (a) reactions, (b) symmetry, (c) energy, (d) hand calculation, (e) zero pivot, (f) mesh refinement, (g) units and (h) element force against reaction.

  • forgotten coupling terms in assembly (wall truss). Finds: (a) reactions. Overlooks: (c) energy.
  • wrong sign in \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) (wall truss). Finds: (a) reactions, (c) energy, (d) hand calculation. Overlooks: (e) zero pivot.
  • \(20\) kN instead of \(10\) kN in \(b_2\) (bridge). Finds: (b) symmetry, (d) hand calculation. Overlooks: (a) reactions, (e) zero pivot, (f) mesh refinement.
  • coordinate \(z = -1{,}4\) m instead of \(-1{,}5\) m (space truss). Finds: (b) symmetry. Overlooks: (a) reactions.
  • missing movable support (bridge). Finds: (e) zero pivot. Overlooks: not tried.
  • half model with a wrong support (bridge). Finds: (d) hand calculation. Overlooks: (a) reactions.
  • mixed units (wall truss). Finds: (d) hand calculation, (g) units. Overlooks: (a) reactions, (b) symmetry, (c) energy, (f) mesh refinement.
  • pin model instead of welded nodes, or neglected bar weight. Finds: none. Overlooks: (a) reactions, (b) symmetry, (c) energy, (d) hand calculation, (e) zero pivot.
  • coarse mesh for a bar with a load along its length (hanging bar). Finds: (f) mesh refinement, (h) element force against reaction. Overlooks: (a) reactions.

7.10.3 Model of a model (model modela)

All the checks work inside the model. They check whether the program computes what the model says, not whether the model says what is true in reality. The first kind of errors is in the computation, and ONATE1 separates them by source (ONATE1 §3.13, PDF pp. 134-139): discretization error, error of the approximation of the geometry, error in computing the element integrals, error in solving the system and error of the constitutive equation. In this chapter we met three. Discretization: the force at the clamp is \(40{,}06\) N with one element instead of \(60{,}10\) N (section 7.4.3). Integration: one Gauss point gives an internal mechanism (section 7.4.2). Solving the system: poor conditioning of the matrix and rounding (ONATE1, PDF pp. 137-139), measured by the sensitivity number (definition 6.31), for \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of the wall truss \(9{,}14\), so without trouble. An error of the constitutive equation, a wrong \(E\), is found by no test of the computation. ONATE1 writes of it that a wrong determination of the material parameters "can lead to larger errors than those induced by all the error sources mentioned in the previous sections" (PDF p. 139).

The second kind of errors is in what the model is: a truss of pins is an idealization (definition 4.4) that no test of the computation sees. Two examples that we can estimate with the numbers from the book. The first is the pin model of the wall truss. In section 5.14.3 we computed the same truss with welded nodes: the displacement of node \(C\) differs by \(0{,}0013\) %, and the forces in the bars by less than \(0{,}3\) N from \(13\,333\) and \(16\,667\) N, that is by less than \(2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of their values. The second is the neglected weight of the bridge bars. The total length of the bars is \(10 \cdot 3 + 5 \cdot 3 + 6 \cdot 4{,}243 = 70{,}46\) m, their weight \(70{,}46\ \text{m} \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 5{,}39\) kN, and the loads \(50\) kN, so the weight is \(10{,}8\) % of the loads. With welded nodes the difference of the forces is of the order \(10^{-5}\), with the weight of the bars of the order \(10^{-1}\). If we compute with a model that does not take the weight into account, checks (a) to (e) are still satisfied. An error of the model shows itself only in a comparison with a measurement, as we planned for the beam in section 5.15.2.

7.11 Connections (povezave)

The abbreviations of the courses are the same as in section 1.19.

  • Element matrix, assembly and supports: beam and frame elements with the rotation of a node (MK, AK, chapter 12, route (b) from section 7.5.1), elements for a continuum and the test with a small sample (patch test) (AK, chapter 15, ONATE1 §3.9, PDF p. 126), elements for heat conduction (AK, VT, chapter 14), where assembly is repeated with temperatures as the unknowns.
  • The mass matrix of a bar element and vibration of trusses (DSK, chapters 10 and 13).
  • Banded and sparse solution of large models (AK, chapter 17), modal reduction (DSK, chapter 21).
  • Symmetry and antisymmetry of structures (MK, AK, chapter 19).
  • Trusses and optimization of the cross-sections of their bars (MK, chapter 29).
  • Compliant links of robots (DSK, chapter 28): an element with free nodes has a rigid motion in which nothing deforms and there is no force, like the unsupported bar in section 7.3 (SHABANA, PDF pp. 280-281). SHABANA removes the rigid motion of an element with reference conditions that fix relative to what the displacement is measured (SHABANA §6.2, PDF p. 286). This is similar to the supports in section 7.3, but not the same: a support pins the body, while a reference condition only decides what we count as deformation, and the rigid motion is described by other coordinates. The link with compliant mechanisms as structures with intended mechanisms is not supported by the sources of the chapter, so we do not state it.
